section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description:
A social media and microblogging platform whose geotagged posts have been the single most-used named data source in this literature by a wide margin. Twitter's relevance to mobility research rests on a specific mechanic: a small, historically stable fraction of tweets carry precise geographic coordinates -- cited repeatedly across this corpus as roughly 1-3% of total tweet volume (individual papers report 1.5%, 1.6%, 1.65%, and similar figures over different years and samples) -- and this geotagged subset can be pulled, historically for free, via a public developer API capped at approximately 1% of the platform's total real-time volume (the 'Streaming' or 'Standard' API), or purchased in bulk as a full historical archive through Twitter's former data reseller Gnip. This access mechanism was not static: Twitter removed support for precise geotagging in June 2019, a structural break that several papers flag explicitly as complicating any study spanning that boundary, and API access narrowed considerably further in the years since (outside the window covered by most of this corpus).

Within this literature, Twitter is used across an unusually wide range of applications: individual mobility characterization (radius of gyration, displacement distributions, entropy-based predictability, home/work location inference from posting-time patterns), origin-destination and migration-flow estimation at scales from single cities to entire countries, disaster and evacuation response (hurricanes, earthquakes, wildfires -- tracking who moved, where, and when relative to an event), COVID-19 mobility monitoring (a large and recurring use case, given Twitter's continued availability through a period when many commercial mobility products faced separate access constraints), epidemic seeding for metapopulation models (using symptom-related keyword tweets or migration signal to initialize simulations), land-use classification, crime prediction, and tourism and event-attendance studies. Several papers position Twitter specifically as a cheap, fast, globally available complement or validation check against a costlier primary source (mobile-phone CDR, a travel survey, SafeGraph, or Foursquare check-ins) rather than as a standalone mobility dataset.

Twitter's representativeness bias is not a minor caveat in this literature -- it is one of its most consistently and explicitly documented limitations. Papers across very different contexts converge on the same finding: Twitter's user base skews younger, more urban, and more affluent than the general population, with substantial cross-country variation in penetration (near-absent in China, where Weibo is used instead; low in India and most African countries; comparatively high in parts of Europe, the Americas, and Australia). One paper states this plainly: 'Twitter users were a uniformly sampled subset of the actual population, which is not necessarily true.' Validation against independent ground truth is genuinely mixed depending on scale and question: several studies report strong correlations against census, ACS, or national travel-survey data at coarse (state, country, or metro) resolution (r values commonly in the 0.7-0.96 range for aggregate flows or population counts), while correlations weaken noticeably as spatial resolution narrows or as the comparison target becomes more demographically specific. Multiple papers caution against treating Twitter as generalizable on its own -- one states outright that 'geo-located Twitter data are not able to generalize to the entire population,' and another, describing its own data as 'real and messy,' notes that geotagged tweets were never actually collected for the purpose the researchers are putting them to.
accessibility_description: Historically accessible via a public developer API (Streaming/Standard) sampling roughly 1% of total tweet volume, with a separate paid full-archive product (via Twitter's reseller Gnip) available for bulk historical purchase. Access terms are not stable across the period this literature spans: Twitter removed support for precise geotagging in June 2019, and broader API access has narrowed substantially since, so consistent access cannot be assumed across the full corpus of citing papers.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description:
A location-based check-in social network whose voluntary venue check-ins have been the second most-used named data source in this corpus. Foursquare differs from Twitter in a way that shapes almost every paper that uses it: Foursquare's own API has historically restricted direct bulk collection of individual users' check-in histories -- several papers state this explicitly ('Foursquare... does not allow to collect user-level check-in data') -- so the dominant collection method across this literature is not to query Foursquare directly, but to scrape check-ins that users voluntarily chose to cross-post to Twitter, a workaround that itself introduces a further, narrower selection filter on top of Foursquare's own user base (one paper estimates this captures only 20-25% of Foursquare's total users; another puts the cross-posted share as low as 10%). A separate, less-used path exists for venue-level (not check-in-level) data: Foursquare's Places/Search API can be queried directly for venue locations and categories, which several papers use to build land-use or points-of-interest layers without needing individual check-in histories at all.

One specific, large check-in dataset (commonly attributed to Yang et al., spanning April 2012-September 2013: 266,909 users, roughly 33 million check-ins, 3.68 million venues, across 415 cities in 77 countries) recurs as a shared, reused foundation across at least five different papers in this corpus, each applying a different analytical lens to the same underlying check-ins (tourist-trip mining, mesoscopic mobility vector fields, revisitation-pattern clustering, next-place-recommendation embeddings). This matters for interpreting the literature: several seemingly independent findings described below are partially the same data examined differently, not fully independent replications.

Applications span next-location and place recommendation, rank-based and gravity-style mobility models, tourist trip and travel-region mining, urban land-use and activity classification via venue categories, population time-use disaggregation, revisitation and routine-pattern analysis, offender-mobility agent-based simulation, and -- notably for epidemic modeling specifically -- pruning digital contact networks for disease-diffusion simulation, using shared-venue co-location as a proxy for contact.

Foursquare's limitations are, if anything, more severe than Twitter's on two specific dimensions repeatedly documented across papers. First, sparsity: check-in histories are described consistently as sparser than comparable passive location data (mobile-phone logs, GPS traces), with a strongly skewed usage distribution -- roughly 20-40% of users in several studies generate only a single check-in, while a small minority generate the bulk of all check-ins. Second, and distinctively, check-ins are an *active, voluntary* signal rather than a passive one: users choose what to check into, which means Foursquare data systematically over-represents notable, checked-in-worthy venues and under-represents routine locations -- several papers note explicitly that users rarely check in at home ('a vast majority of 4sq users never check in at their homes'), which is the opposite bias direction from passive mobility data that tends to capture home/routine locations most reliably. On top of these mechanical biases, the same demographic skew documented for Twitter recurs here -- younger users, geographic concentration in large or tech-forward cities, and in some studies a male skew -- with one paper stating plainly: 'there may be a strong demographic bias in the community of Foursquare users.'
accessibility_description: Foursquare's own API has historically restricted direct bulk collection of individual check-in histories; the dominant workaround in this literature is scraping check-ins voluntarily cross-posted to Twitter (capturing an estimated 10-25% of Foursquare's total user base, itself already a non-representative subset). Venue-level metadata (locations, categories) is more directly queryable via Foursquare's Places/Search API.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description:
A photo-sharing platform whose geotagged photographs capture a location only at the moment a photo is taken and uploaded -- not a continuous trace -- making it structurally different from Twitter's geotagged posts or Foursquare's check-ins, even though it is grouped with them here. This distinction matters for what Flickr is actually good at measuring: multiple papers converge on the same characterization, that Flickr data 'mostly reflects activity during leisure traveling and sightseeing' rather than routine, everyday movement, and that people 'generally take photos in interesting locations.' One paper notes explicitly that Flickr 'more often reveals people's travel mode' than home-anchored daily movement. This makes Flickr, among the sources in this corpus, unusually well-suited to studying discretionary and tourism-related travel specifically, and correspondingly weaker for the routine, everyday mobility that CDR or GPS-trace data captures more directly.

Unlike Twitter and Foursquare, Flickr is the most-used source in this corpus that is genuinely openly accessible: several papers draw on large, publicly released research corpora built directly from Flickr's own data, most prominently the Yahoo Flickr Creative Commons 100 Million Dataset (YFCC100M, spanning 2004-2014, roughly 20% geotagged), which recurs across multiple independent papers in this corpus, alongside at least one other large merged public corpus (over 130 million geotagged photos and videos, 2005-2014) reused by two further papers. As with Foursquare's shared 'Yang et al.' dataset, this means some of the apparently independent findings below are analyses of overlapping underlying photo collections rather than fully separate replications.

Applications span human-mobility and origin-destination modeling (validated in one case against the UK National Travel Survey, correctly predicting closer-to-survey OD flows than random in 92 of 100 trials), international travel-flow estimation (correlated r=0.78 against World Bank departure statistics), tourism and points-of-interest attractiveness studies, home-location inference methods, and social-ecological interaction mapping between residents and visitors at natural/recreational sites. Validation against independent ground truth is generally reasonable at the aggregate flow level, but at least one paper flags a specific methodological weak point: simple home-location heuristics (most-photographed location, etc.) are markedly less stable on Flickr than on comparable financial-transaction location data (a similarity measure across five heuristic methods varied 10-20% on Flickr versus only 1-9% on bank-transaction data), consistent with Flickr's event-driven rather than routine-anchored sampling.

Flickr's geographic and demographic coverage is heavily skewed toward Europe and North America, with explicit, repeated notes that Flickr is comparatively unpopular in China (one paper documents a substantial mismatch between Flickr-derived and actual Chinese departure statistics specifically attributable to this) and under-used in much of the Global South. Several papers also note the data is comparatively sparse per user, sometimes requiring multi-year (even decade-long) collection windows to assemble enough signal for a given analysis, and that Flickr's own userbase over-represents technologically engaged, camera-carrying users -- 'crowdsensing' bias toward whichever events or places already attract concentrated photographic attention.
accessibility_description: Publicly accessible via Flickr's own photo-search API (registration required for an API key) and, more commonly in this literature, via large public research-released corpora built from Flickr's data -- most notably the Yahoo Flickr Creative Commons 100 Million Dataset (YFCC100M) -- with no formal data-sharing agreement typically required.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description:
The register's own description of Facebook as check-in-style location data used alongside Foursquare turns out to be misleading once the actual full-text papers are read: in this corpus, essentially no paper analyzes individual Facebook check-ins at all. References to 'Facebook Places' or Facebook check-ins appear only as generic, passing mentions in background sections listing location-based social networks; one paper uses a Facebook-derived ego-network graph purely as a generic benchmark for a community-detection algorithm, unrelated to mobility. What Facebook actually is, in practice, across this literature, is Meta's own aggregated 'Data for Good' products -- Movement Maps, Disease Prevention Maps, and population-density tiles built from opted-in users' location data and released to approved researchers, not individual check-in records at all.

Consistent with this, nearly every citing paper is a COVID-19-era mobility study (2020-2022): tracking population decline and redistribution during UK lockdowns, decomposing mobility into workday/weekend/holiday components across France, Italy, and Spain, measuring counter-urbanization in Belgium and Thailand, and partitioning geography into COVID-relevant regions via a Social Connectedness Index (a friendship-network measure, not a mobility measure). One paper -- a comparison of mobility data sources for measles transmission modeling in Zambia -- stands apart from the COVID cluster and is a source of a separate, important finding elsewhere in this review: outbreak-seeding predictions from the same epidemic model varied sharply depending on which mobility data source (including this Facebook product) was used to parameterize it.

Coverage is consistently a small, non-representative fraction of the true population -- typically single-digit to low double-digit percentages per geographic tile and time window across the countries studied (roughly 3-9% in the UK, France, Italy, and Spain; higher platform penetration in Belgium and Thailand but similarly limited effective coverage after location-sharing opt-in is accounted for). Every paper documents the same demographic skew: users are described as skewed toward younger and middle-aged groups, systematically under-representing children and the elderly, and Facebook's own location-sharing feature is opt-in, adding a further, compounding selection layer on top of ordinary platform demographics. Meta's own privacy protections -- differential-privacy noise and a hard minimum-count threshold (data suppressed below roughly 10 people per tile or trip) -- introduce a further, structural bias: in the Zambia study, this threshold caused estimated departure probability to read as exactly zero for most of the 48 least-populated districts studied, not because mobility was actually absent but because it fell below the reporting floor. Validation against independent ground truth is mixed: one Italian study found Facebook-derived population estimates broadly consistent with national statistics after correction, while a separate five-network comparison study found Facebook's regional partitioning to be the least effective of all the human-behavior networks tested for explaining COVID-19 case-rate differences.
accessibility_description: Not accessible as raw check-in or user-level data. Meta's aggregated 'Data for Good' products (Movement Maps, Disease Prevention Maps, population-density tiles) are made available to approved researchers and public-health partners under a data-sharing agreement, with differential-privacy noise and a minimum-count reporting threshold applied before release.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description:
A crowdsourced, volunteered geographic information (VGI) project (founded 2004 at University College London) that maps streets, buildings, points of interest, and land use worldwide through open, freely editable tagging. Unlike almost every other source in this document, OpenStreetMap does not itself record movement or presence -- it records the built environment that movement happens within. Consistent with this, no paper in this corpus uses OpenStreetMap as a mobility-trace source; every citing paper uses it as a spatial reference layer supporting a mobility analysis built from a genuinely different primary data source (mobile-phone records, gravity/radiation model outputs, or a large-scale synthetic-population simulation).

Two related, specific uses recur. First, several papers use OSM's road network to classify or contextualize movement recorded elsewhere -- inferring a mobile-phone user's transport mode from a cell tower's proximity to a highway versus a bus corridor, or supplying a road-network distance proxy for school-proximity estimation in a large-scale (350-million-agent) synthetic-population health simulation. Second, several papers use OSM's points-of-interest and land-use tags (shops, restaurants, parks, recreation areas) as explanatory variables to diagnose *why* an independently-built mobility model succeeds or fails at particular locations -- one detailed study of gravity, radiation, and intervening-opportunity models across 112 wards in Oxfordshire found that trip destinations the models most underestimated had markedly higher density of certain POI tags (clothing retail density +250%, fast-food/restaurant density +~100% relative to well-predicted destinations), using OSM tag density as a diagnostic lens on model error rather than as an input to the mobility model itself. (This Oxfordshire study appears twice in the underlying literature -- an arXiv preprint and its published Royal Society Open Science version -- as the same study, not an independent replication.)

One paper uses OpenStreetMap differently again: openstreetmap.org has historically hosted user-uploaded, user-tagged GPS traces (distinct from the map data itself), and one study repurposes a set of these self-tagged tracks (walk/run/bike/car) as ground-truth labels for training a movement-type classifier -- an incidental use of OSM's platform rather than its map database.

The clearest, most consistently documented limitation is geographic unevenness in coverage: because OSM is built entirely from volunteer contribution, data density tracks contributor density, not population or importance. Multiple papers state this directly -- 'much less data about smaller or poorer places' -- and one paper specifically excluded certain transport-infrastructure tags from its analysis because of their poor and inconsistent coverage. A related structural pattern, noted in one paper's own tag-usage audit, is a long-tailed distribution of tag types: of over 800 distinct tag types found in one regional extract, just 21% of tag types accounted for 99% of all tag uses, meaning most of OSM's tagging vocabulary is used rarely and inconsistently even where the map itself is well-populated.
accessibility_description: Freely accessible worldwide via bulk data downloads or the Overpass API, under an open database license (ODbL); no registration, data-sharing agreement, or cost required. Data completeness is uneven and depends entirely on volunteer contributor density in a given area.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description:
A publicly released GPS trajectory dataset collected by Microsoft Research Asia, tracking a modest number of volunteer participants (reported variously as 165, 178, or 182 depending on which analysis subset a given paper draws from -- these are all filtered slices of the same underlying release, not independent datasets) continuously over multi-year periods (April 2007 through roughly 2011-2012 across most citing papers), predominantly in and around Beijing with some trajectories from other Chinese provinces. In total the dataset spans on the order of 17,000+ individual trajectories, 1.2 million kilometers, and 48,000+ hours of tracked movement. Unlike the social-media-derived sources elsewhere in this document, GeoLife is continuous, passive GPS tracking at high sampling frequency -- most trajectories are sampled every 2-5 seconds -- giving it a fundamentally different density and quality profile from check-in or geotagged-post data.

The register's own description (a benchmark for trajectory analysis using curvatures, stop-points, and velocities) captures one real use but understates the breadth: across the papers in this corpus, GeoLife functions almost entirely as a standard, convenient algorithm-development benchmark rather than as a source used to answer substantive behavioral or epidemiological mobility questions directly. Citing papers use it to validate trajectory-prediction models, next-location Hidden Markov Models, missing-data imputation methods, spatio-temporal entropy and curvature-based trajectory analysis, periodic-pattern detection algorithms, and stay-point/point-of-interest inference for disease-monitoring algorithms -- a real, valuable role, but one where GeoLife is the testbed for a method rather than the object of a mobility finding in its own right.

Two limitations recur specifically because of how the data was physically collected. First, GPS signal is lost whenever a participant enters a building, since the tracking device shuts off automatically and users frequently forgot to re-enable it on leaving -- creating systematic gaps that, notably, mean home and other indoor, significant locations are comparatively unreliable to estimate from GeoLife specifically, since only outdoor 'outings' are consistently captured (a different mechanical route to a similar home-location weakness noted for check-in-based sources elsewhere in this document, though for a device/hardware reason here rather than a voluntary-disclosure one). Second, the dataset carries no socio-demographic information about its participants at all, which multiple papers note explicitly as a constraint on generalizing any GeoLife-derived finding to a broader population.
accessibility_description: Publicly released by Microsoft Research Asia and freely downloadable, with no registration or data-sharing agreement required.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description:
A location-based check-in social network that was acquired by Facebook in December 2011 and shut down in 2012 -- unlike Twitter, Foursquare, or Facebook, Gowalla no longer operates at all, so every paper in this corpus necessarily works from a frozen, historical snapshot rather than any live collection. Several distinct snapshot datasets circulate and are reused across different papers rather than one single canonical release: a widely-used academic dataset built from a breadth-first-search (BFS) crawl of the friend graph and check-ins (391,223 users, 26.3 million check-ins, collected over a few weeks in 2011), a smaller California-focused dataset from the same era (the 'Cho et al.' dataset, ~145,000 events, ~7,600 users), a larger 27-million-check-in dataset spanning 2009-2011 used alongside Foursquare and Altergeo in one multi-platform study, and an independently collected Texas-specific sample (14,592 residents). As with the reused datasets seen in Foursquare and Flickr, some findings attributed to different papers here are analyses of the same or overlapping historical snapshots, not independent samples of Gowalla's user base.

Because the standard collection method for the largest, most-reused dataset is a breadth-first-search crawl of the social (friend) graph, this corpus documents a distinct sampling bias not seen elsewhere in this document: BFS crawling is explicitly described as 'highly biased toward nodes with high degree,' meaning well-connected, highly social users are systematically over-represented relative to the platform's true user base. This sits alongside, rather than replaces, the ordinary demographic skew also documented here -- one paper using a Texas-specific sample notes its userbase skewed toward younger, male, and Hispanic individuals. Some releases also provide no explicit user location or profile information at all, and because check-ins were only ever visible for locations a user chose to share, no paper has access to check-ins withheld by privacy settings.

Unusually for a defunct platform, Gowalla's actual use in this literature matches the register's own description reasonably well: the majority of citing papers genuinely do use Gowalla to validate human mobility models against real check-in-derived network and geographic structure -- next-check-in-location prediction, nearby-stranger and location recommendation, an explicit 'Friendship Mobility Model' benchmarked against a random-walk baseline in mobile network simulation, and social-activity-travel participation modeling using shared check-ins between friends as a proxy for co-located social activity. One paper's own motivating analysis, using Gowalla check-ins directly, found that individual users' location preferences drift substantially over time (under 30% check-in overlap between the first and second half of a user's own history for the large majority of frequent users sampled) while the *time-of-day* at which a given location is visited stays comparatively fixed across different visitors -- a specific, quantified behavioral regularity that directly informed that paper's own model design.
accessibility_description: The platform itself no longer exists (shut down 2012), so no live collection is possible. All current use draws on one of several historical check-in/friend-graph snapshots collected via API or BFS crawling between roughly 2009 and 2011, most of which have been released freely for academic research (e.g., the widely-used SNAP-hosted Gowalla dataset).

section: Aggregated Commercial Mobility Products
description:
A commercial location-data provider that derives aggregated mobility products from anonymous mobile-device GPS signals -- point-of-interest visit counts, census-block-group-level origin aggregates, and a bundled 'Social Distancing Metrics' product -- rather than raw individual trajectories. Every citing paper in this corpus is a COVID-19-era study (predominantly 2020-2021), using SafeGraph to construct contact networks or mobility indices for epidemic modeling, measure stay-at-home compliance, or validate mobility change against case counts, across geographies ranging from individual cities (Philadelphia, New York City) to a four-state Midwest comparison (Illinois, Ohio, Michigan, Indiana) to nationwide county-level analysis.

The device sample is consistently described as roughly 5-10% of the US population (some individual census tracts as low as 1%), but -- distinctly from the open or registration-based sources elsewhere in this document -- the exact underlying collection and sampling methodology is proprietary and undisclosed. One paper states this plainly: 'the exact data collection and sampling processes remain unclear.' SafeGraph applies its own privacy-driven suppression rule on top of this already-partial sample, explicitly excluding any census block group's visit count if fewer than two distinct devices visited an establishment in a given month -- a specific, documented threshold distinct from (and lower than) the roughly-ten-device thresholds seen in Facebook's comparable products. An independent audit of SafeGraph's own panel, cited by one paper, found underrepresentation of older and non-white individuals specifically in point-of-interest-level analyses, and the standard home-location method used across these papers (most common overnight census-block-group location over a trailing six-week window) inherits whatever bias exists in the underlying device panel.

Where SafeGraph has been checked against independent ground truth, results are informative but uneven: one comparison against New York City taxi trip data found a strong overall correlation between SafeGraph device counts and actual trip volume (Pearson r≈0.95), but noted the product 'excels at car-dependent-commute trips' while specifically underestimating pedestrian-heavy trips -- a mode-dependent bias worth flagging for any application weighing walking-based short-range movement. During the sharpest phase of the pandemic, one national-scale study using this data documented daily US visits falling from roughly 45 million to 25 million and mobility-network connectivity (county-to-county link persistence) falling by roughly 20%, illustrating the scale of disruption the product was able to capture even under its sampling constraints. The recurring caution across nearly every paper is the same: mobile device location, however large the underlying panel, remains only a proxy for actual human contact, and single mobility metrics derived from it were found in one study to be insufficiently sensitive to capture the full complexity of post-reopening human interaction on their own.
accessibility_description: A commercial product, typically made available to researchers through an academic or research access program rather than a public API. The underlying device panel and sampling methodology are not publicly disclosed, and a privacy-driven suppression rule withholds any census block group with fewer than two visiting devices in a given month.

section: Aggregated Commercial Mobility Products
description:
A passive, primarily Android-based smartphone location-tracking service whose access mechanism is unlike any other source in this document: there is no research API or data-sharing agreement at all. Individual users export their own historical location data themselves via Google's 'Takeout' tool, and every study in this corpus compiles data this way -- recruiting a small number of participants who voluntarily retrieve and share their own exports. Consistent with this, sample sizes here are far smaller than any other source in this document: the largest study uses 25 participants, most use fewer, and one uses only 5 phones. This corpus consists almost entirely of methods papers actively testing whether Google Location History (GLH) is even usable and reliable for mobility research, rather than papers using it to answer a substantive mobility question -- GLH is treated throughout as a novel, still-unvalidated data source, with one paper describing it explicitly as 'greatly underutilized.'

The validation evidence across these papers is genuinely mixed, not simply positive or negative, and the two most direct validation studies reach different conclusions because they test different things. One study, focused on longer-duration and international mobility, found strong spatial agreement against dedicated GPS tracker ground truth (median distance 64m, roughly 85% grid-cell agreement at 100m resolution) and found that GLH captured 41 international trips that a parallel GPS tracker missed entirely and a travel survey only partially captured (18 of 41) -- suggesting real value specifically for long-duration, low-burden tracking that dedicated devices and self-report cannot sustain. A second study, focused on fine-grained trip reconstruction against a prescribed 12-day itinerary, found GLH correctly matched only 51% of ground-truth locations and 32% of ground-truth trips, concluding plainly that 'GLH data does not currently appear to be an adequate tool for travel diary data collection.' Read together, these are not contradictory findings so much as evidence that GLH's fitness depends heavily on the specific mobility question being asked -- it may suit coarse, long-horizon movement tracking better than fine-grained, short-window trip diaries.

Recording frequency is inconsistently documented across papers -- one states outright that 'it is not clear exactly how frequently GLH records data' -- and appears to vary with movement state (as often as every 30-60 seconds while moving, every 1-5 minutes while stationary, in one paper's direct observation) and by phone hardware, with one paper noting performance 'varies greatly by phone brand,' with iPhones performing worst (consistent with GLH being fundamentally an Android-oriented service). One pilot study estimates that up to 61% of the US population may technically have GLH data available, but actual usable data still depends on active retrieval and sharing consent, which several papers note explicitly excludes less tech-engaged, lower-income, and other vulnerable populations -- a real gap between broad technical availability and what is actually collectable for research. More than one paper also flags privacy risk specifically: linking this kind of high-resolution personal mobility history to identifiable demographic information raises meaningful re-identification concerns.

Two of the papers here (using near-identical dataset descriptions, 16,855 location records collected over one month) appear to draw on the same or closely related underlying data collection for semantic trajectory pattern mining -- not fully independent studies.
accessibility_description: No research API or data-sharing agreement exists. Individual users export their own historical location data via Google's Takeout tool; researchers compile datasets by recruiting participants who voluntarily retrieve and share their personal exports.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description:
A short-term rental platform whose scraped listings, guest reviews, and declared user profile residence have been used, in the single paper citing it here, to reconstruct international tourism flows. The platform is large in principle (roughly 7 million listings across more than 100,000 cities worldwide as of the study), but the actual analysis works from a single snapshot in time (12 September 2019 for the featured Iceland case study, expanding outward to over 3.1 million comments from 1.94 million people covering 100,000 locations globally to build a broader origin-destination network of trip flows between destinations). Trips are reconstructed by chaining a single user's dated comments across different listings when the gap between them is under 30 days, and the resulting flow counts correlate reasonably well with official tourism-arrival statistics overall, though the fit was notably weaker for a few specific countries (UK, Japan, Norway).

Because collection is a single retrospective snapshot, historical listings that have since been removed are invisible, likely underestimating true historical platform usage, and a booking's declared account holder does not necessarily represent every person actually in that travel group. Declared residence in a user's profile is self-reported and reflects only their most recently listed home, not necessarily their residence at the time of a given trip.
accessibility_description: Scraped from Airbnb's own public listing and review pages via a custom, publicly released collection script; no formal API agreement was used, but scraping at scale required recursively subdividing search areas to work around the platform's own display caps.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A check-in-based location-based social network popular in the Russian-speaking market, used in the single paper citing it here alongside Foursquare and Gowalla to test whether a general check-in mobility framework ('SPoT') holds up across a geographically and culturally different platform. Altergeo's dataset in that study is the smallest of the three (roughly 700,000 check-ins from 49,000 users over two years, 2010-2012, filtering down to a few thousand usable arrival sequences and contact pairs), and its role is specifically to demonstrate the underlying modeling framework's flexibility across markets rather than to support any Altergeo-specific finding.
accessibility_description: Access mechanism is not stated in the citing paper; treated the same as Foursquare and Gowalla check-in data in that study, suggesting a comparable collection method.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A now-defunct location-based check-in social network, used in the single paper citing it here as one of several national check-in datasets (alongside Twitter and Gowalla) to calibrate a combined 'Travel and Friendship' agent-based mobility model. The Brightkite sample used is comparatively small (58,000 users, split roughly 27,000 UK and 1,300 Germany), and the paper reports this specific dataset gave the weakest model fit of the sources it tested (error 0.39, versus better fits on other platforms in the same study).
accessibility_description: Register data marks this source as open; the citing paper does not detail its own collection method beyond identifying geotagged check-ins by country.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: Google's venue and review platform, used in the single paper citing it here as a direct comparison point against Foursquare for building 'interest networks' (graphs connecting neighborhoods where the same users are active). In that study's two city case sites, Google Places produced a broadly similar but not identical partition of the city compared to Foursquare's own network (moderate agreement between the two platforms' derived neighborhood clusters), and the paper notes the same demographic-skew and data-age caveats documented for Foursquare apply equally here. One specific asymmetry the paper flags: Foursquare's data includes users' inferred home and workplace locations, which Google Places' review-based data does not provide.
accessibility_description: Accessed via Google's own Places API; register data marks this as proprietary access, consistent with a commercial platform API rather than an open research release.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description:
A photo and video-sharing social network whose geotagged posts share a specific collection advantage over Twitter, noted explicitly in one paper here: Instagram's API historically allowed retrieval of a user's *entire* post history within a defined search area, rather than only a small percentage sample of real-time volume, though collection is constrained to circular search areas of a limited radius (up to 5,000m per query in one study) rather than the rectangular bounding boxes usable on Twitter. In practice this makes Instagram a denser, though still geographically bounded, alternative to Twitter for a given study area -- one Amsterdam case study collected nearly 16 million posts this way over a three-month window.

A second, France-based study using Instagram specifically for tourism-flow analysis in Biarritz documents two structural limitations that recur for photo/post-based mobility data generally: EXIF location metadata is stripped on upload (posts are geotagged only via an explicit, separate tagging step, not embedded GPS), and the platform's own geotag-suggestion algorithm is opaque, meaning researchers cannot fully audit how candidate locations are selected or ranked. That paper also notes Instagram's public API access for this kind of research use was closed after 2016, meaning any Instagram-based study using API access rather than third-party scraping tools is necessarily working with older data.
accessibility_description: Public post retrieval within defined geographic areas was possible via Instagram's own API prior to 2016; access for this kind of bulk geotagged-post collection has since closed, and more recent studies rely on third-party scraping tools instead.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A check-in dataset crawled from a location-based social network's open API in China (the register's dataset name reflects the crawling study's author rather than naming a distinct platform), used in the single paper citing it here to study gender differences and city-level variation in check-in behavior. The dataset (nearly 90,000 anonymous users, 2.4 million check-in records collected over three months in 2012, concentrated in Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou, and Hangzhou) shows the same heavily Pareto-skewed usage pattern documented for other check-in platforms in this document: the most active 20% of users generated roughly 80% of all check-ins, while the majority of users were comparatively inactive. The paper's one specific substantive finding -- that female users were more active than male users in this sample -- is worth noting as a rare instance in this literature of a check-in platform showing the opposite gender skew from the male-leaning pattern documented for several other LBSN sources in this document.
accessibility_description: Crawled via an open API; the specific platform and its ongoing access terms are not clearly identified in the citing paper.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A purpose-built WeChat mini-program (a lightweight in-app tool within China's dominant messaging platform, which the citing paper notes had 440 million daily active users as of August 2020) designed specifically to collect research-grade mobility data: logins, profile views, weather checks, geotagged check-ins, and self-reported mood, alongside a separate demographic questionnaire. Unlike the repurposed social-media platforms elsewhere in this document, LBSLab was built for this specific research purpose rather than scraped after the fact -- but the resulting sample in the one paper citing it here is correspondingly small and narrow: 467 student users at a single university (Fudan University, Shanghai) tracked over 11 days.
accessibility_description: A purpose-built research data-collection tool, not a public platform; participation requires being recruited into the specific study that deployed it.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A geo-tagged photo-sharing platform, used in the single paper citing it here to reconstruct human mobility traces from geo-tagged photo metadata -- the same general approach applied to Flickr elsewhere in this document, using the same clustering and gravity-based place-association methodology, applied here to a Budapest case study (177,496 photos yielding 4,061 usable daily movement traces). The paper reports the same category of limitation documented for Flickr: photo coordinates and timestamps can be altered by the user or corrupted by camera/software workflow quirks, requiring a noise-filtering step (a speed-threshold heuristic) before traces are usable.
accessibility_description: Publicly accessible geo-tagged photo metadata, collected via the same general approach as Flickr in this literature.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A location-based mobile game, studied in the single paper citing it here not as a location-data source in its own right but as a behavioral intervention whose effect on players' real-world mobility is measured using two separate underlying data sources: a smartphone-app-usage dataset (Carat, providing coarse cell-tower-level rather than GPS-level location, and only while the app happens to be running) to identify roughly 4,000 confirmed players, and a separate geotagged-Twitter sample to identify a broader set of self-identified players discussing the game. The paper's central finding is a measurable mobility effect: players showed roughly 1,400 additional steps per day attributable to the game, and the radius-of-gyration distribution for confirmed players and non-players was similar in shape but shifted, consistent with genuinely increased movement rather than a change in movement pattern.
accessibility_description: No direct access to in-game player location data; the study infers player mobility indirectly through a separate smartphone-app-usage panel and cross-referenced Twitter posts, not through any data the game itself made available.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A check-in app (Foursquare's dedicated check-in-only spinoff), studied in the single paper citing it here via a specifically manual collection method: because Twitter's free-tier search only returns results from the past week, and Swarm check-ins are only visible in this study through their cross-posted appearance on Twitter, the researchers manually collected check-ins in real time over two separate seasonal windows in Melbourne (3,332 check-ins total) rather than using any bulk retrieval method. This is the most labor-intensive collection method for any check-in-style source in this document, and it caps the achievable sample size accordingly.
accessibility_description: No direct API access used; check-ins were collected manually as they appeared, cross-posted, on Twitter's public search, due to Twitter's own free-tier limits on retrieving older data.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description:
A Chinese microblogging and social media platform, described directly in this literature as 'the Chinese equivalent of Twitter,' and used specifically because Twitter and Instagram have negligible penetration in China -- one paper states this plainly: in China, neither can be used as an urban-dynamics proxy 'since the penetration rate is negligible,' making Weibo the necessary regional substitute rather than an arbitrary alternative choice. All empirical studies here focus on major Chinese cities (Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen), generally over multi-month to multi-year windows, and applications include activity-type classification from post text (using a BERT-based classifier to sort posts into categories like entertainment, eating, and studying), entertainment-venue check-in pattern analysis, individual movement-prediction modeling, and sensitivity testing of how far mobility-pattern indicators (like radius of gyration) shift depending on the spatial grid size chosen for analysis.

One study conducted during the COVID-19 outbreak explicitly could not include Wuhan data at all -- not due to access restrictions, but because so many people stayed home that the resulting mobility signal was 'too small to test.' The same demographic caveat recurs across these papers as with other social platforms: users are described as skewing young, and one paper notes explicitly that relying on Weibo as the sole data source for a study means the resulting sample 'was restricted and perhaps skewed,' since no independent source was available in the same study to cross-check it. Weibo also appears in a sixth, non-empirical context: one dissertation lists it only as a planned data-source module in a multi-platform system architecture (alongside Twitter and Instagram), without ever running an actual Weibo-specific case study.
accessibility_description: Accessible via Weibo's own API for geo-enabled posts and check-ins, though as a China-specific platform its terms and researcher access are distinct from the globally-focused platforms elsewhere in this document.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A now-defunct location-based check-in service. This document could not include any content beyond the register's own summary description, because the single paper that cites this source -- and the only lead available for it -- was one of the small set of papers this review's retrieval effort was ultimately unable to obtain despite exhaustive search (confirmed closed access with no mirror or preprint found anywhere). Per the register, the paper investigated urban mobility patterns and how the spatial distribution of places shapes movement, using check-in records not restricted to any particular transportation mode.
accessibility_description: Access mechanism could not be determined -- the citing paper itself could not be retrieved for full-text review despite exhaustive search.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: Two genuinely unrelated uses of Wikipedia recur in this small corpus, and they should not be read as two versions of the same application. The first, more conventional use treats Wikipedia as a general crowdsourced encyclopedic corpus (over 3 million pages) to semantically enrich points of interest identified from other mobility data -- matching a location's Wikipedia content (by category or by title) to characterize what kind of place it is. The second use is entirely different in kind and unique among every source in this document: rather than studying present-day mobility, one paper mines the biographies of historically notable people (drawing on the Pantheon dataset of over 11,000 individuals with Wikipedia pages in at least 25 languages, spanning from 3500 BC to 2010 AD) to extract dated migration and relocation events -- exile, imprisonment, career moves -- across history, filtering to a working subset of roughly 2,400 biographies active between 1900 and 1950. This is the only historical (rather than contemporary) mobility source in this document. The extraction pipeline used for this purpose is imperfect specifically on recall -- it correctly identifies migration events it does catch with high precision (0.86), but a substantial share of real movements described in a biography (an estimated 40%) are missed entirely, typically because they are described implicitly or split across sentences the extraction pipeline does not connect.
accessibility_description: Fully open and freely accessible; no registration or agreement of any kind is required to use Wikipedia's content for either application described here.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A business review and check-in platform. Despite three papers nominally citing it, no paper in this corpus actually analyzes Yelp data directly -- every citing instance is a brief, generic background mention grouping Yelp alongside other location-based social networks (Foursquare, Twitter, check-in services generally) as an example of the category, with no Yelp-specific numbers, methodology, or findings reported anywhere in the underlying full texts.
accessibility_description: Register data marks this source as open; no paper in this corpus describes an actual collection method, since none performs a Yelp-specific analysis.

section: Location-Based Social Networks and Check-In Applications
description: A video-sharing platform, used in the single paper citing it here in an application unique among the LBSN sources in this document: publicly available, geo-referenced videos explicitly tagged as recorded in Africa (113,157 unique records) are mined to reconstruct continent-level travel routes, identify major travel hubs via density-based clustering, group similar routes between those hubs, and infer likely timing and transportation mode by combining video timestamps with other online data sources (such as identifying specific carriers, flights, or bus lines). This is the only application in this document treating video (rather than text, photo, or check-in metadata) as the primary evidence for a mobility trace, and the only one focused specifically on a continent-scale, cross-border travel-route reconstruction rather than city- or country-level individual mobility.
accessibility_description: Publicly accessible, geo-referenced video metadata; no registration or agreement required.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: An Austrian mobile network operator, used in the single paper citing it here to reconstruct subscriber trajectories from network-side handover (HO) and location-area-update events -- signals generated automatically as a phone's connection shifts between cell towers, not GPS. The paper's core contribution is comparing two fundamentally different ways of turning these coarse tower-connection events into an actual road-network path: mapping each handover to a specific estimated position using either simple Voronoi tessellation (treating each tower's coverage as a fixed polygon) or a more detailed network-planning coverage-prediction model (with and without a building/terrain obstruction layer), then snapping the resulting path onto OpenStreetMap roads and adjusting positions using known speed limits. The coverage-prediction approach, especially with buildings included, produced meaningfully better position accuracy than plain Voronoi tessellation across four real test drives, though the paper notes this improvement is limited by only having access to freely available network data -- it could not incorporate proprietary antenna configuration or transmit-power details that would likely improve accuracy further. Handover event spacing itself varies sharply by area type (roughly 625m apart in semi-rural areas versus 283m in urban areas), reflecting differences in tower density rather than anything about the traveler.
accessibility_description: Network-side handover and location-area-update event data from a core mobile network; not a public dataset, accessible only through a research relationship with the operator.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description:
China's dominant search and mapping company, whose 'heat map' and migration-index products (built from smartphone location signals, not cellular signaling in the traditional CDR sense) are used across four papers here almost entirely for population-flow and mobility-change analysis around major events -- a small city's hourly population clustering, national migration scale during COVID-19 travel restrictions, and a machine-learning model that uses Baidu's own flow index as a prediction target for a nighttime-satellite-imagery-based mobility estimate. The most epidemiologically direct finding here comes from a national migration-network study built around the initial COVID-19 outbreak: out-migration from Wuhan correlated strongly with subsequent case counts in other cities (r=0.943), and roughly 69% of people leaving Wuhan stayed within the same province -- a concrete, quantified example of exactly the kind of mobility signal a metapopulation epidemic model needs to capture. A separate study found the national migration scale fell by roughly 37% during the ordinary Spring Festival travel period that year, and by a further 78% once nationwide traffic control measures were imposed.

Two structural limitations recur. First, being smartphone-app-derived, Baidu's products explicitly cannot capture movement by anyone without a smartphone or without the relevant app installed -- one paper states this plainly as a coverage gap, not merely a sampling nuance. Second, temporal availability is inconsistent and event-driven rather than continuous: one paper notes the migration-index product has genuinely limited data availability across the calendar year, concentrated mainly around major travel periods like the Spring Festival and National Day, rather than being available as a continuous year-round signal.
accessibility_description: A commercial product (heat maps and migration index), accessed through Baidu's published data/API products rather than a formal research data-sharing agreement in the papers reviewed.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: A Colombian mobile network operator, whose call detail records were shared under a research agreement in the single paper citing it here to identify aggregate urban mobility patterns in Santiago de Cali over two pre-pandemic months (January-February 2020). A specific, structural limitation distinguishes this source from most other CDR providers in this document: the data provided to researchers was already compressed and reduced by CLARO itself for privacy and transfer-efficiency reasons before it ever reached the research team, meaning the granularity available for analysis was constrained by the operator's own processing choices, not just by standard privacy-driven aggregation applied at analysis time. The resulting dataset is explicitly restricted and non-shareable beyond the original research partnership.
accessibility_description: Call detail records shared under a specific research agreement with the operator; the data was pre-compressed by CLARO before release and is not shareable beyond the original research partnership.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description:
A major Chinese mobile network operator, whose mode-identified signaling data (able to distinguish road, rail, and air travel) is used across two papers here for city-flow network analysis and a study of neighborhood-level gentrification. The flow-network study, covering 36 major and 298 other Chinese cities, found a substantial and consistent weekday-versus-weekend difference in movement volume (total weekend flow roughly 28.5% higher than weekday flow across the sampled weeks), a pattern worth keeping in mind for any model treating mobility as constant across the week. The gentrification study uses a stricter definition of presence -- a stay of more than 30 minutes at the same location constitutes a 'residency record' -- to isolate an 'activity population' distinct from simple presence, tracking how a specific neighborhood's demographic composition shifted between 2017 and 2021.

Both papers note the same category of limitation common to signaling-based CDR sources generally: one describes the data as having 'some defects, such as bias and poor accuracy,' with travel routes frequently fragmented into disconnected pieces rather than clean end-to-end trips, and neither paper has access to individual demographic attributes (age, gender, occupation) due to privacy restrictions on what the operator releases.
accessibility_description: Mobile signaling data provided by the operator for research use; individual demographic attributes are withheld for privacy.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: A Caribbean mobile network operator, whose data underpins one of the most-cited studies of disaster-driven population displacement in this literature: a study tracking 1.9 million mobile subscribers in Haiti for 42 days before and 341 days after the January 2010 earthquake. Port-au-Prince's population fell by roughly 23% within 19 days of the earthquake, and despite the disruption, the paper found individual movement remained highly predictable overall (a predictability measure peaking at 0.85), including successfully anticipating a surge of return travel around the following Christmas and New Year holidays using the same predictive model. The paper is explicit about two real constraints: the mobile network itself suffered reduced capacity immediately after the earthquake (potentially undercounting movement during exactly the period of greatest interest), and location is recorded only once per day (at a subscriber's first call), meaning any movement within a single day is invisible to this data by construction. The paper also flags, rather than resolves, an open question directly relevant to any disaster-response application of mobile data: how well movement patterns of people who own mobile phones actually represent the movement of those who do not.
accessibility_description: Data provided through a direct research collaboration with Digicel (the largest mobile operator in Haiti at the time), not a public product.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: A commercial location-data provider, used in the single paper citing it here to compute footfall (human activity) metrics across Greater London from anonymous mobile-phone GPS trajectory data, explicitly provided under GDPR-compliant terms. The dataset covers over 1.1 million users (representing 41.6% of the provider's UK-wide panel) across more than 400 observation days spanning the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, and documents footfall falling by roughly 65% following the UK's first lockdown -- a concrete measure of the scale of behavioral disruption over that period. Unlike the network-signaling CDR sources elsewhere in this document, this is genuine GPS-level location data (not tower-connection events), giving it finer spatial resolution, at the cost of being a commercial product rather than a direct operator research partnership.
accessibility_description: A commercial GPS location-data product, provided under explicit GDPR-compliant terms; accessed via a commercial arrangement rather than a public API or open dataset.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: A GPS trajectory dataset from the Italian mobile operator Tim, covering roughly 5% of mobile devices in the Bologna metropolitan area, used in the single paper citing it here to reconstruct individual movement paths and characterize their statistical properties across the city's road network (finding, for example, that path lengths follow an exponential distribution with a characteristic scale of about 3.8km, while path durations follow a power law). The paper states plainly that this roughly 5% sample penetration, while sufficient for reconstructing individual paths and studying aggregate mobility structure, is not sufficient for directly studying road-level traffic congestion, which would require much denser coverage.
accessibility_description: GPS trajectory data from the mobile operator Tim, made available for this specific research use; not a public dataset.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: A Japanese mobile-network-derived population statistics product (from NTT DOCOMO, roughly 44% of the Japanese mobile market as of the citing paper), used in the single study here to extract urban mobility flow patterns. MSS is structurally distinct from every other cellular source in this document in one specific way: it provides only population *snapshots* (a count of how many people are in a given area at a given hour), with no movement or origin-destination information built in at all -- the paper's own methodological contribution is inferring directional flow indirectly, by applying an optimal-transport (Wasserstein-distance) calculation between two consecutive hourly snapshots to estimate the most likely underlying movement that would explain the population shift. This inference approach fit the data reasonably well during daytime hours (goodness-of-fit 0.73 for the 7-8am snapshot) but considerably worse late at night (falling to 0.47 for 10-11pm), when population movement is less structured and harder to infer from population counts alone. The paper also notes that privacy-driven aggregation causes a specific, acknowledged loss the source calls 'trip loss.'
accessibility_description: A commercial population-statistics product (trademarked 'Mobile Spatial Statistics') from a mobile network operator; population snapshots only, with no movement information provided directly.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description:
A multinational mobile network operator (operating in France as Orange and in Senegal as Orange/Sonatel), whose call detail records and network signaling data anchor five papers here spanning Côte d'Ivoire, France (Paris and Rhône-Alpes regions), and Senegal -- several drawing on Orange's well-known 'Data for Development' (D4D) Challenge releases, a rare case in this document of an operator making CDR-derived data available specifically for open research competitions rather than only through bilateral agreements.

Two papers here provide unusually rigorous, direct validation of CDR-derived mobility against independent ground truth. One compares an Île-de-France origin-destination matrix built from base-station signaling data against a large household travel survey (18,000 households, 150,000 trips) -- overall trip counts matched within about 9%, with a strong linear relationship (R²=0.96), but individual origin-destination pairs could disagree by as much as 70-80%, a sharp reminder that a good aggregate fit does not guarantee good fit at finer geographic detail. A second, similarly structured validation in the Rhône-Alpes region against a regional travel survey found comparable overall agreement but systematic direction-dependent errors: mobility to and from Lyon specifically was under-estimated, while zones sharing long borders were prone to over- or under-estimation depending on boundary effects in how signaling events get assigned to a zone.

A Côte d'Ivoire-focused paper studying rural visibility documents a specific, quantified urban-rural asymmetry directly relevant to representing short-range mobility: 70% of calls originating in rural areas stayed within the vicinity of the same cell tower, compared to only 23% of urban-originated calls -- meaning rural movement is systematically harder to detect from this kind of network data not because rural people move less, but because rural cell towers cover much larger areas, making genuine local movement look identical to staying still. This same paper's dataset is further restricted to subscribers who remained active for the entire 150-day capture window, meaning anyone who joined or left the network mid-study is excluded by construction.

A recurring, explicit limitation across these Orange-based studies, stated directly in one paper: CDRs are 'cheap and efficient' but their sampling is inherently sparse and irregular, since a subscriber's location is only recorded when they happen to make a call or send a text -- unlike GPS-based sources, there is no way to increase temporal resolution without the subscriber generating more network activity.
accessibility_description: Some data (the D4D Challenge releases) made available specifically for open research competitions; other studies here draw on bilateral research agreements with Orange or its regional subsidiary Sonatel. Not a standing public API.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description:
The mobile services arm of Telecom Italia (roughly 30% of the Italian mobile market across both papers citing it), providing aggregated network density data -- a count of how many phones are attached to a given network node, not any individual device tracking -- used here for Milan-wide people-flow inference and a Venice pedestrian-movement study during major festival crowds (Carnival and the Redentore festival). The Milan study applies the same general optimal-transport (Wasserstein-distance) technique seen elsewhere in this category to infer directional flow from successive density snapshots, since the raw signal only shows how many phones are present, not which direction anyone moved. The Venice study is validated directly against manual volunteer pedestrian counts on a bridge, and found its raw sample penetration (an estimated 3-4% of pedestrians) needed a substantial recalibration factor (roughly 1.6x) to approach the ground truth, still leaving an average error of about 20% -- a concrete illustration of how much correction a sparse cellular sample can require even after recalibration.

Both papers note the same structural constraint: because this system counts phones attached to network nodes rather than tracking GPS, localization is lost entirely if a phone is off or silent for more than roughly six hours, and Venice's narrow, dense streets specifically degraded signal reliability relative to the Milan study.
accessibility_description: Aggregated cellular network density data (counts of connected phones per node, not individual tracking), made available for these specific research collaborations.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description:
Italy's largest mobile operator (variously reported as 30-40% national market share across the five papers citing it), whose call/SMS traffic and network activity data anchor a genuinely varied set of studies -- youth-concentration mapping via SMS usage patterns, international-community detection via country-code call activity, one of the earliest and most-cited urban 'big data' collaborations (MIT's 'Real Time Rome' project, using four months of Rome network activity from 2006), individual resident-mobility decomposition in Milan via independent component analysis, and urban 'vitality' proxying via aggregated call-activity records across six cities.

A specific, recurring methodological point across several of these papers: raw call/SMS traffic volume ('Erlang' units, one person-hour of phone use) does not directly represent the number of distinct people generating that traffic, since usage intensity varies by age and socio-professional group -- one paper uses this explicitly, treating SMS traffic specifically as a proxy for younger (15-24 age) populations precisely because that group's SMS usage pattern differs systematically from the rest of the population, rather than treating traffic volume as a simple headcount. The Real Time Rome paper states the underlying privacy protection plainly: 'deducing individual identities from the data collected and stored in the system is impossible,' since Erlang measurements are aggregate network load, not individually attributable call records. The international-community study notes its own generalizability limit explicitly -- restricted to a single city and a two-month observation window.
accessibility_description: Call/SMS traffic and network activity data made available through Telecom Italia's own research lab (its 'Semantics and Knowledge Innovation Lab') or direct research collaborations (e.g. with MIT); not a standing public product.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: A Chilean mobile network operator, whose data underlies one of the largest single cellular datasets in this document: 31 billion Extended Detail Records (XDRs) from 5.4 million users, spanning nearly seven months (late February through September 2020) during Chile's COVID-19 pandemic response, used in the single paper citing it here to build daily mobility indices for each of Chile's 346 comunas (municipal-level administrative units, varying widely in size, averaging roughly 2,200 km² with substantial variation). A record is generated automatically roughly every 15 minutes whenever network traffic crosses a threshold, and a subscriber's home location is assigned to whichever cell tower shows the most nighttime activity. The paper reports a notably strong validation against the 2017 national census (R²=0.96) for its resident-population estimates, one of the stronger census-validation results among the cellular sources in this document. One structural limitation is worth flagging clearly: the paper's own indices are built from tower-to-tower transitions, which capture 'movement' in a network sense but do not necessarily correspond to a semantically meaningful trip.
accessibility_description: Extended Detail Records provided through a research collaboration with Telefónica Chile; not a public dataset.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: A Hungarian mobile network operator (Magyar Telekom, roughly 45% of the national telecom market), used in the single paper citing it here specifically to study tourist mobility -- filtering to users whose SIM cards are registered to a foreign country, rather than studying the general population. This source carries an unusually strict, legally-driven access constraint distinct from every other operator in this document: under Hungary's own legal interpretation of GDPR, individual mobility histories cannot be reconstructed across more than a 24-hour window at all -- device identifiers are deliberately rehashed daily, meaning even with full data access, no one (including the operator itself) can link the same device's location across different days. The paper states this constraint plainly: individual mobility histories 'are not even available for research purposes.' Exact tower coordinates are also withheld as a business secret, a further access restriction beyond the privacy constraint itself.
accessibility_description: Cellular location records for foreign-SIM users, made available for this specific study; legally restricted to 24-hour windows under Hungary's interpretation of GDPR, with device identifiers rehashed daily and exact tower coordinates withheld as a business secret.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: Location data from Tencent's messaging platforms, used in both papers citing it here specifically to study China's Chunyun (Spring Festival travel) period -- the annual mass migration considered one of the largest recurring human movement events in the world. One paper tracks the evolution of migration network structure across 337 cities between 2015 and 2019, finding the busiest ('diamond network') connections grew from carrying about 405 million to 604 million people, eventually accounting for over 80% of all national travel flow during the period studied. A second paper, using a machine-learning approach on a single Spring Festival period (2018), found that plain geographic distance alone accounted for the majority (57%) of predictive importance in explaining inter-city connection strength -- distance still dominates even in an era of high-speed rail and air travel. Both papers note the same structural limitation: the underlying data is aggregated at the city level with no individual passenger characteristics, meaning there is no way to distinguish a tourist from someone returning home for the holiday within the same flow count.
accessibility_description: A commercial big-data platform product (Tencent's Location Big Data Platform), accessed for these studies rather than through a standing public API.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description: Tencent's population-flow product, derived from location-call requests generated by its WeChat and QQ platforms (a combined user base described in one paper as over 1 billion monthly active WeChat users and 800 million QQ users, generating roughly 55 billion location-call requests per day), used across three papers here for national and regional city-network analysis in China -- eigenvector-centrality mapping of national urban hierarchy, asymmetric flow-pattern analysis specifically around Spring Festival in the Yangtze River Delta region, and a graph neural network model simulating inter-city population flows more broadly. Every paper here is explicit about the same underlying scope limitation: this reflects the movement of Tencent's own social-media users specifically, not a verified count of actual travelers, and one paper notes its own dataset is further limited to only the top-10 cities by volume per transport mode, not a complete national picture.
accessibility_description: A commercial migration/population-flow product (Tencent Migration Platform), accessed for these studies as a data product rather than through a standing public API.

section: Mobile Network Operator Data (CDR and Cellular)
description:
A multinational mobile network operator, whose Italian and pan-European network probe data underlie three papers here -- a COVID-19 mobility dashboard built for Italian public authorities, an earlier Milan traffic- and crowd-estimation study, and a broader case study on data-sharing practices for telecom data across Vodafone's European footprint. The Italian COVID-era study (Vodafone holding 'a market share of over 20%,' described as fairly homogeneous across age and gender) is explicit about the exact privacy mechanics applied before any data reaches researchers: individual SIM-level metrics are aggregated to municipality level, and any origin-destination movement count below 15 trips between two towns is removed entirely (a specific k-anonymity threshold) -- and the paper states plainly that the underlying granular metadata itself cannot be shared or replicated externally at all, since both GDPR and Italian privacy law prohibit it, a stronger access restriction than most other sources in this document, where at least some raw or lightly-aggregated data can sometimes reach researchers under agreement.

The earlier Milan study is one of the more rigorously validated cellular-mobility papers in this document: its traffic-index estimates were checked against multiple independent big events (concerts, football matches) and against subway ridership figures, generally landing within single-digit percentage error of reported ground truth (e.g., estimating a specific concert's attendance within 9% of the reported figure), though the paper is candid that 'no strong validations' of its own origin-destination algorithm exist against a proper census baseline, since the most recent Italian census data available at the time was already a decade old.

The pan-European case study adds a structural point relevant to interpreting any cellular-derived mobility number across the countries in this document generally: spatial precision is fundamentally limited by local network-tower density, which itself tracks population density -- meaning rural and low-population areas are systematically both under-represented (due to aggregation thresholds) and less precisely located (due to sparser tower coverage) than urban areas, a compounding, not merely additive, disadvantage for exactly the areas most likely to be small subpopulations in an epidemic model.
accessibility_description: Network probe/CDR/XDR data made available through direct collaborations with Vodafone; underlying granular metadata is explicitly non-shareable outside these arrangements under GDPR and Italian privacy law.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description:
A citizen-science smartphone app, launched by the BBC alongside a documentary, that collected hourly location logs and self-reported contact data from nearly 29,000 UK volunteers over roughly one month in 2017. Unlike most GPS trajectory datasets in this document, this one was purpose-built to feed directly into an actual epidemic model, and the single paper citing it here does exactly that: it uses participants' movement relative to their home location to build an age- and gender-structured, gravity-style kernel describing how contact probability falls off with distance between subpopulation patches (aggregated to over 9,300 model patches nationally), and combines this with self-reported contact data to construct age-structured contact matrices -- both components a metapopulation epidemic model needs directly, not merely descriptive mobility statistics.

The paper is candid about representativeness limits specific to this kind of voluntary participation: app users likely do not represent a random sample of the population even setting aside ordinary mobile-phone-ownership bias, participants who joined early in the campaign may differ systematically from those who joined later, and the minimum age restriction (13+) underrepresents the youngest age groups this kind of contact data would ideally cover. A specific methodological limitation is also flagged: the underlying contact data records that a contact occurred, but not the distance at which it occurred, and a default setting on the app's own age-reporting slider is noted as a likely source of bias in the estimated ages of reported contacts.
