accessibility_description: Collected via a purpose-built citizen-science app; not a standing public dataset, accessed through the research team associated with the original BBC collaboration.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A US severe-weather-warning smartphone app, whose location-tracking feature (over 300 users, 14 months) is used in the single paper citing it here to study how people actually move in response to real weather alerts -- most concretely, a documented case where 24 app users received an alert during a tornado near Mansfield, Texas, and their subsequent movement was directly observable in the data. Location is logged frequently (every 2 minutes, or whenever the device moves 100m, 250m if the app is running in the background), yielding over 5.5 million high-quality GPS points overall, which the paper converts into discrete activity 'duration records' (a start time, end time, and duration per stay) rather than working with raw point-by-point coordinates directly. The main documented limitation is data-quality drift rather than sampling bias: unusually long 'duration' records occur specifically when a user stops carrying their phone or disables location services, meaning the data cannot distinguish 'stayed in one place for a long time' from 'stopped generating usable location data.'
accessibility_description: GPS location data from app users, made available for this specific research use; not a public dataset.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A well-known, openly released GPS trajectory dataset covering 538 San Francisco taxis over one month (May-June 2008), used in the single paper citing it here to study the regularity of individual route-level movement decisions. After filtering, roughly 287,000 usable trajectories remained, and the paper's central method (using information-theoretic entropy over a discretized road-grid to segment each trajectory into more and less predictable sub-segments, achieving substantial compression of the resulting representation) is a route-level analysis technique rather than a mobility-volume or origin-destination study, distinguishing this use from most other GPS trajectory sources in this document. The paper flags one specific representativeness caveat worth keeping in mind for any generalization beyond taxis specifically: cab mobility may have systematic properties -- shaped by professional driving patterns and passenger-seeking behavior -- that differ from private-vehicle movement.
accessibility_description: A well-known, openly released academic dataset; freely available for research use.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A small drone-video pedestrian trajectory dataset collected on the campus of Dalian University of Technology, used in the single paper citing it here purely as a validation benchmark for a generative pedestrian-behavior model -- not as a source for any substantive mobility finding in its own right. The dataset consists of only three small case studies (each involving two or three pedestrians walking together or navigating around an obstacle), and its role is entirely to provide ground-truth trajectories that a generated (simulated) trajectory can be numerically compared against.
accessibility_description: A small, specific benchmark dataset; register data marks it as open.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description:
A large-scale, globally distributed smartphone-usage research panel (over 17,000 volunteer participants across more than 150 countries), used across both papers citing it here to infer individual life patterns and daily routines from anonymized WiFi scan records rather than GPS coordinates directly -- a device periodically records which WiFi access points are visible nearby, and researchers use the resulting pattern of recurring access-point sightings to infer 'stay places' and, from there, daily routines. Most participants contributed data for less than six months, and both papers restrict their core analysis to the smaller subset who contributed longer (2,500 users with 3+ months in one paper; 746 users with 6+ months in the other), out of the full panel.

Both papers converge on the same fundamental epistemic limitation, and state it with unusual directness for this literature: because there is no independent ground truth for what a WiFi-derived 'stay place' or 'life pattern' actually corresponds to in reality, one paper states outright that its own conclusions are, 'at best, an educated guess.' A second, related limitation is that WiFi-inferred locations carry no semantic information at all -- the method can detect that someone regularly visits a particular place, but not what kind of place it is (home, work, or something else) without further inference. One paper's home-detection specifically failed for 59 users due to gaps caused by devices being turned off or WiFi disabled.
accessibility_description: A large volunteer research panel; anonymized WiFi scan data made available to researchers through the Device Analyzer project, not a standing public API.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A major Chinese ridesourcing (ride-hailing) platform, whose GPS trajectory and order-timing data are used in the single paper citing it here to build a city-scale traffic-flow network for Chengdu and predict vehicle dwelling time (accounting for traffic congestion) from ride order patterns. The paper describes this as first-hand, massive-scale proprietary data, combining both the spatial GPS trajectory and the temporal order information directly from the platform -- a genuine industry data partnership rather than a scraped or publicly released dataset.
accessibility_description: Proprietary ride-order and GPS trajectory data obtained directly from the Didi platform; not a public dataset.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A crowd-sourced seismic early-warning smartphone app with a large global user base (over 5 million participants), whose incidental location pings -- generated for earthquake-detection purposes, not mobility research -- are repurposed in the single paper citing it here to test a location-density estimation method on a genuinely sparse, error-prone real-world dataset (a Rome-specific subsample of 1,188 smartphones over four months, with a median sampling interval of roughly 30 minutes and around 20m location precision). The paper states its motivating limitation plainly: this kind of location data is 'sparse in time and affected by non-negligible errors,' and a device generates no signal at all when powered off or without an internet connection -- making this less a mobility dataset than a stress test for methods that need to work despite highly irregular, incidental location signals.
accessibility_description: Location pings incidental to a crowd-sourced seismic-detection app; access mechanism for research use is not detailed in the citing paper.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: Two large-scale, year-long tracking pilot studies conducted by Swiss Federal Railways (SBB), used in the single paper citing it here as one of six benchmark tracking datasets to validate a general-purpose, parameter-free mobility stop-detection and trajectory-segmentation method. The citing paper provides no further detail about this specific dataset's own content or findings beyond identifying its origin -- its role here is purely as one of several validation datasets for a method whose real contribution lies elsewhere.
accessibility_description: Access mechanism not detailed in the citing paper; originated from a Swiss Federal Railways research pilot.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A human mobility benchmark dataset (the naming suggests an associated data challenge or competition), used in the single paper citing it here to compare three different ways of representing the same underlying movement data as a graph, evaluated using two graph neural network architectures. The dataset itself is substantial for a benchmark -- 100,000 individuals' trajectories over 90 days, at 30-minute temporal resolution and 500m spatial grid cells -- but the paper notes two real constraints on how far its findings generalize: the data represents a single mid-sized city, and a held-out 'hidden' test portion (presumably reserved for a formal competition leaderboard) was not available to this paper's own authors.
accessibility_description: A benchmark dataset, likely tied to a data challenge; full access terms and whether a held-out test portion is publicly available are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A large benchmark mobility dataset spanning four Japanese cities, used in the single paper citing it here to evaluate a model (CLIFT) for transferring learned mobility patterns across cities -- both from one city to another and within a single city. Scale varies substantially across the four cities (one city alone contributes 100,000 users and 111.5 million records over 75 days at 30-minute, 500m-grid resolution; the smallest city contributes only 3,000 users), and the cross-city transfer approach produced a modest but real accuracy improvement over a single-city-only baseline. A specific and unusual access constraint is worth noting: the identities of the four cities and the exact collection period are deliberately undisclosed for privacy reasons, which the paper itself flags as a real limitation -- it prevents researchers from linking this mobility data to any external land-use, demographic, or geographic reference data for that city, since the city cannot be identified in the first place.
accessibility_description: A benchmark dataset with city identities and exact collection period deliberately withheld for privacy; access terms beyond this are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: Two genuinely separate small-scale South Korean trajectory datasets share this name across the papers citing it here, and should not be read as one dataset. The first (10 graduate students tracked over two months via combined GSM/WiFi/GPS logging every two minutes) is used to compare first- and second-order Hidden Markov Models for next-location prediction. The second, collected separately in 2011 by 8 users at Yonsei University in Seoul (1,848 identified activities across 800 individual trajectories), is used to validate a geometric trajectory-clustering method (identifying critical turning/curvature points via convex hulls) for detecting human movement patterns. Both are small, pilot-scale benchmark datasets used to validate specific algorithms rather than to support a substantive mobility finding, and one paper explicitly describes LifeMap generally as 'commonly considered a reference benchmark' in this line of research -- suggesting the name may refer to a small family of similarly-constructed pilot datasets rather than one single, canonical release.
accessibility_description: Two apparently distinct small research datasets sharing this name; access terms are not detailed in either citing paper.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A purpose-built smartphone app ('MTL Trajet'), deployed in Montreal to collect fine-grained GPS trajectories directly labeled with the traveler's transportation mode and trip purpose at the time of collection -- a genuine advantage over most GPS sources in this document, which require inferring mode and purpose after the fact rather than having the traveler report it directly. The single paper citing it here (nearly 35,000 trajectories collected over one month in 2017, across 7 travel-mode and 9 activity-purpose categories) uses this labeled data specifically to train and benchmark a generative adversarial network for synthesizing realistic synthetic trajectories.
accessibility_description: Collected via a purpose-built municipal research app; access terms are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: Trip data from a Chinese dockless bike-sharing service (Mobike), used in the single paper citing it here alongside taxi trip records and points-of-interest data to build and compare urban 'spatial similarity' networks -- essentially asking whether neighborhoods that are structurally similar in how bike-share trips connect them are also similar in other urban respects (the paper validates its bike-share-derived network against a points-of-interest dataset focused on education and training institutions). Over a two-month collection window (August-September 2016), the resulting Mobike-derived movement network was found to lack the structural regularity seen in the same city's taxi-derived network -- a direct, quantified illustration that different mobility modes within the same city can produce genuinely different network structures, not just different volumes.
accessibility_description: Access mechanism not detailed in the citing paper.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A commercial location-data provider, whose high-resolution, opt-in GPS trajectory data for Great Britain (2019) is used in the single paper citing it here to study how urban environment use differs by neighborhood deprivation level. Raw trajectories are converted into 'semantic' trajectories -- home and work locations identified at a coarser spatial resolution, individual stops identified at a finer one -- and enriched with area-level functional classification. The resulting population distribution correlates strongly with official UK population statistics (ρ=0.94), a comparatively strong validation result among the commercial GPS-based sources in this document. The paper is direct about the source's two structural limits: Spectus provides no demographic information about the individuals behind each trajectory at all, and because participation is opt-in, the underlying panel is self-selected rather than randomly sampled.
accessibility_description: A commercial GPS location-data product; accessed via a commercial license from Spectus.ai, not a public dataset.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A well-known, openly released public dataset of one week of GPS trajectories from 10,357 Beijing taxis (February 2008), amounting to roughly 15 million GPS points and 9 million kilometers of total travel. The single paper citing it here is the dataset's own user guide/documentation paper rather than an independent analysis, describing its basic technical properties (an average sampling interval of about 177 seconds, average distance of roughly 623 meters between consecutive points) for other researchers to use the release correctly.
accessibility_description: A well-known, openly released public research dataset from Microsoft Research Asia.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: An openly available pedestrian trajectory benchmark specifically built around interaction scenarios (people walking as leaders and followers, in groups, or navigating around obstacles), used in the single paper citing it here purely as a cross-validation benchmark for a generative pedestrian-trajectory model -- the same validation role the DUT dataset plays for the identical paper, but for interaction-heavy scenarios specifically rather than simple movement.
accessibility_description: A well-known, openly released academic pedestrian-trajectory benchmark.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A wireless-network trace dataset (over 13 million recorded events across 275 network nodes and 524 WiFi access points, collected over two months) used in the single paper citing it here to simulate and validate a mobility-prediction algorithm that combines an individual's own movement history with the movement of their socially related contacts (identified via shared WiFi access-point co-location) to improve prediction accuracy beyond what either source alone would achieve.
accessibility_description: An openly available academic wireless-network trace dataset from UC San Diego.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: The ride-hailing platform, mentioned only as a generic example of 'social-sensing' trajectory data in the single, brief passing reference citing it here -- a background chapter listing data source types, with no independent Uber-specific analysis, numbers, or methodology reported anywhere in the text.
accessibility_description: Register data marks this as proprietary; no specific access details are given, since the citing text does not perform an independent analysis using Uber data.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: Not a mobility dataset at all, but a geospatial indexing system (a way of dividing the globe into a consistent grid of hexagonal cells at various resolutions), open-sourced by Uber and used in the single paper citing it here as pure spatial infrastructure -- assigning home, school, and workplace anchor locations for an entire large synthetic population in a contact-network epidemic simulation, at a resolution of roughly 0.8 square kilometers per cell, with workplace assignment weighted by daytime population density from a separate gridded-population source. This belongs conceptually closer to the geographic-reference sources elsewhere in this document than to the mobility-trace sources it sits alongside here, since it provides spatial structure rather than any movement or presence data itself.
accessibility_description: An open-source geospatial indexing library, freely available with no registration or agreement required.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: Uber's aggregated, depersonalized travel-time data product (derived from GPS records in the company's own taxi-hailing vehicles), used in the single paper citing it here as an independent validation source for a gravity-model origin-destination matrix built instead from OpenStreetMap road data, for Amsterdam (divided into 181 transport zones) and a smaller comparison city. The gravity-model estimate showed only moderate agreement with the Uber-derived ground truth (R²=0.6), which the paper attributes to high variability in the underlying data and the inherent roughness of a road-network-only origin-destination estimate -- a useful illustration that Uber Movement, despite being aggregated and privacy-protected, still functions as real ground truth against which a purely structural model can be checked and found only partially accurate.
accessibility_description: A free, publicly released aggregated data product from Uber, made available without a commercial license for many cities.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description: A Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) offering, studied in the single paper citing it here as one of six benchmark tracking datasets used to validate a general-purpose mobility stop-detection and trajectory-segmentation method. Data was collected via a companion GNSS tracking app ('MyWay') from participants in a three-month treatment-versus-control study design (871 enrolled, 161 in the treatment group receiving the MaaS offer, 710 in a control group, with 498 completing the study) -- a genuine behavioral-intervention study design, distinguishing this from the purely observational tracking datasets elsewhere in this category, though the citing paper here uses it only as one validation case for its own trajectory-segmentation method rather than analyzing the intervention itself.
accessibility_description: GNSS tracking data from a specific MaaS research study; not a public dataset.

dataset_name: Advan Research Corporation (via Dewey Data platform)
section: Aggregated Commercial Mobility Products
description: A commercial mobile-device foot-traffic data provider, accessed through the Dewey Data marketplace platform, used in the single paper citing it here to build time-varying county-to-county mobility matrices for a COVID-19 transmission model covering the earliest weeks of the pandemic in the US (late February through mid-April 2020). The paper's substantive finding using this data is epidemiologically significant in its own right: the inferred dispersion parameter describing how superspreading-prone transmission was shifted sharply after lockdown measures took effect (from k=0.50 before to k=1.3 after, where a lower k indicates transmission concentrated in fewer, larger spreading events) -- a concrete, quantified example of how mobility-driven contact structure itself, not just contact volume, can change during an intervention.
accessibility_description: A commercial point-of-interest visit dataset, accessed through the Dewey Data marketplace rather than a direct provider relationship or public release.

section: Aggregated Commercial Mobility Products
description:
Anonymized origin-destination mobility flows built from opted-in Google Location History users, used across the two papers citing it here to study seasonal mobility patterns in Kenya and to test whether satellite nighttime-light imagery can serve as a cheaper proxy for this kind of mobility data across 12 African countries. The Kenya study surfaces a specific, quantified finding directly relevant to a static-rate assumption used elsewhere in this document's companion review: movement showed clear seasonal peaks in August and December, coinciding with school holidays, and one county (Machakos) alone accounted for roughly 75% of movement into Nairobi -- a concrete example of exactly the temporal heterogeneity that challenges treating short-range mobility as constant year-round. The nighttime-light comparison study found its proxy worked reasonably well in rural and peri-urban areas but broke down specifically in dense urban settings, where light intensity and actual mobility volume decouple.

Both papers note the same access and representativeness constraints: this dataset reflects only smartphone users who actively opted into Google's Location History feature (off by default), access to the raw data requires direct permission from Google, and the released figures are themselves passed through a differential-privacy noise mechanism -- meaning what researchers see is already a privacy-protected approximation, not the underlying flow counts directly. One paper notes explicitly that mobile phone ownership bias means representativeness likely varies by location, not just by demographic group uniformly.
accessibility_description: Requires direct permission from Google to access; built from an opted-in user subset and released only after differential-privacy noise is applied.

section: Aggregated Commercial Mobility Products
description:
Google's flagship COVID-era mobility product -- daily percentage-change indices, relative to a pre-pandemic baseline, across six place categories (retail & recreation, grocery & pharmacy, parks, transit stations, workplaces, and residential) -- and one of the most widely cited data sources in this entire document. This entry merges what were initially two separate register rows ('Google Community Mobility Reports' and 'Google Mobility Report'), once it became clear the papers citing the latter were using specifically the 'residential' category of this same six-category product, not a separate Google release. Across the five papers now grouped here, uses range from directly rescaling an origin-destination matrix for a Mexico City COVID transmission model, to comparing this index against independent GSM-derived mobility and self-reported survey data, to a literature-scoping review finding well over 100 relevant epidemiological modeling papers had used this product as either a direct model input or a validation check against model output.

A recurring and unusually pointed criticism across these papers is Google's own lack of transparency about how the index is actually calculated: one paper states plainly that 'Google provides no further details on the measure itself,' and another notes the 'retail & recreation' category specifically likely underestimates true shopping-related mobility, without a way to verify by how much. The standard caveats recur here too -- the underlying panel is opt-in (Location History off by default), aggregated at a level that prevents any individual-level analysis, and passed through differential-privacy noise before release. One paper's own scoping review notes a further, structural limitation for longitudinal epidemic modeling specifically: most published applications of this data focus on a single pandemic wave, limiting insight into how the underlying mobility-to-transmission relationship might shift across multiple waves or variants.
accessibility_description: Freely published by Google with no registration or agreement required, though the underlying calculation methodology is not disclosed and the published figures are already aggregated and privacy-noised before release.

section: Aggregated Commercial Mobility Products
description: A Meta (Facebook) product recording the daily number of Facebook users traveling between countries, used in the single paper citing it here to build country-level mobility networks (via graph embedding) for modeling cross-border COVID-19 spread over a two-year window (March 2020-April 2022). This source provides a concrete, named illustration of a platform-access gap flagged more generally elsewhere in this document for Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram: Facebook itself is banned in several countries, China explicitly named among them, creating genuine missing data for those specific international routes rather than merely a demographic sampling gap -- the absence isn't a matter of who opted in, but of the platform simply not operating there at all. As with other Meta products in this document, the data reflects only users who chose to share their location.
accessibility_description: A Meta data product made available for this research use; not a standing public dataset.

section: Aggregated Commercial Mobility Products
description:
A genuinely unusual mobility proxy among every source in this document: motion-sensor readings from smart home thermostats, voluntarily contributed by users through ecobee's 'Donate Your Data' (DYD) research program (over 1 million total users, including more than 172,000 Canadian households, of which 12,252 across four provinces were used in the single study citing it here). Rather than tracking where someone goes, this source measures the inverse -- how much motion is detected inside a home over each 24-hour window, used as a direct proxy for residential occupancy (how much time people spend at home) rather than inferring it indirectly from the absence of an outdoor signal, as every phone-based source in this document must do. The resulting daily indoor-activity measure correlated moderately with Google's own residential mobility index over the same period (r=0.67-0.73) -- meaningful agreement, but far from identical, suggesting the two measures capture related but not equivalent aspects of at-home behavior. The paper notes indoor/in-home mobility remains a generally underexplored complement to the outdoor-movement focus of most mobility data sources.

One process note: the two papers citing this source (and Google Mobility Report above) are a JMIR journal publication and its preprint counterpart, reporting identical content and figures -- they should be read as one study appearing twice in the citation record, not as two independent findings corroborating each other.
accessibility_description: Motion-sensor data voluntarily contributed by smart-thermostat owners through ecobee's Donate Your Data research program; not a public dataset.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: The UK's 2011 national census, used in the single paper citing it here for its aggregated commuting-flow data at Local Authority District level across two English regions (the Northern Powerhouse and Greater South East). The paper builds directed, weighted commuting networks from this data and finds a striking structural difference between the two regions using Shannon-entropy measures: the Northern Powerhouse's commuting network is meaningfully more diverse/less concentrated (entropy 0.91) than the Greater South East's (0.79), and movement in the Northern Powerhouse is more concentrated onto a small number of dominant routes (half of all journeys occur on just 5% of origin-destination links, versus 7% in the Greater South East) -- a concrete illustration that commuting network structure can differ substantially between regions even within the same country and census.
accessibility_description: A national census; commuting flow data is publicly released at Local Authority District level.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description:
A large, ongoing US Census Bureau survey providing detailed demographic and socioeconomic data between decennial censuses. This entry merges what were initially two separate register rows -- 'American Community Survey' and 'American Census Survey (ACS)' -- since ACS is the standard abbreviation for this exact survey and no separate real-world US government survey by the latter name exists; this was almost certainly a naming inconsistency across citing papers rather than two distinct sources.

Across the four papers now grouped here, uses include appending demographic attributes to vehicle-trajectory data to infer trip purpose, synthesizing detailed household-level socioeconomic populations from the survey's public microdata sample (a Bay Area case study working from a roughly 6.1% household sampling rate), and benchmarking county-to-county migration models against other US administrative data sources. One paper is candid that survey data generally carries real 'deficiencies and latencies' compared to more direct measurement, and a separate migration-benchmarking paper notes a structural property that recurs across administrative mobility data more broadly: the overwhelming majority (97.3% in this case) of all possible county-to-county migration pairs record zero measured movement, meaning most of the analytical signal is concentrated in a small number of genuinely active routes.
accessibility_description: Publicly released US Census Bureau survey data, including detailed microdata samples (PUMS), freely available for research use.

dataset_name: Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics
section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: Brazil's national statistics agency, whose 2016 intercity multi-modal transport capacity data (road and river travel, together representing weekly capacity for roughly 78 million passenger-trips, covering an estimated 38.7% of the population) is used in the single paper citing it here as part of a broader mobility dataset supporting a disease-spread model aimed at identifying good locations for early pathogen detection. The paper notes a specific, concrete limitation: this road and waterway mobility data has not been updated since 2016, making it increasingly outdated for current-day applications.
accessibility_description: Publicly released national statistics agency data.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: The detailed 'long-form' component of the US decennial census (distinct from the short-form count everyone receives), used in the single paper citing it here as one of several administrative data sources benchmarked for county-to-county migration modeling. This source carries a specific, severe currency limitation directly stated in the paper: only the 2000 census vintage is still available at county level at all, since the long-form was discontinued after that census and replaced by the ongoing American Community Survey -- meaning any migration model relying on this specific source is necessarily working from data at least two decades out of date, with no documented way to know exactly how its underlying data-suppression procedure works. As with the American Community Survey entry, the same structural pattern recurs here: over 90% of all possible county-pair migration flows are recorded as zero.
accessibility_description: Historical US Census Bureau data (discontinued after the 2000 census); publicly available but not current.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: India's national census (most recently conducted in 2011, covering 28 states, 8 union territories, 640 districts, and over 600,000 villages), used in the single paper citing it here to provide district-level demographic marginal distributions for generating a large-scale synthetic population for an agent-based epidemic modeling framework (BharatSim) -- individual-level census microdata is not publicly available in India, so only these district-wise aggregate marginals are usable directly. The paper is explicit about a real, ongoing constraint this creates: as of the paper's own publication in December 2024, India has not conducted a census since 2011 (the originally-scheduled 2021 census did not proceed), forcing the paper to supplement this 13-year-old data with separate government population projections extrapolated forward in an attempt to approximate the current population structure.
accessibility_description: District-level aggregate marginals are publicly released; individual-level census microdata is not publicly available in India.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: A large Chinese household survey (roughly 133,000 and 127,000 respondents across two waves, 2015 and 2017), used in the single paper citing it here to build a migration-probability matrix and simulate long-run population redistribution across China via a random-walk model calibrated to these survey-derived migration rates. The resulting simulated population distribution matched real population data reasonably closely (deviation of roughly 0.2 in both survey waves), and the paper's own framing of its central finding -- that migration follows a distinct spatial 'agglomeration pattern' -- is a genuinely substantive mobility finding rather than a purely methodological contribution.
accessibility_description: A large household survey; access terms for this specific research use are not detailed in the citing paper, register data marks it as restricted.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: A US Environmental Protection Agency dataset of neighborhood-level built-environment and accessibility metrics, used in the single paper citing it here to enrich vehicle-trajectory data with land-use and accessibility context -- helping validate inferred home and work locations (identified as a vehicle's two most frequently visited locations) against the actual land-use category of those locations, as a plausibility check on the underlying location-inference method.
accessibility_description: A publicly released US government dataset; freely available for research use.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: A Hungarian government administrative database tracking individuals' educational and career trajectories, used in the single paper citing it here to trace roughly 47,000 graduate students from their birth location, through university enrollment, to their eventual workplace -- a genuinely unusual, longitudinal individual-level administrative data source distinct from most cross-sectional survey or census data elsewhere in this document, since it follows the same specific individuals across multiple life stages over more than a decade (2006-2017 for the underlying application records). The paper itself frames Hungary's ability to link these career-tracking and application databases together as a genuinely rare achievement, describing it as among the first such integrated administrative datasets in this research area.
accessibility_description: A government administrative database; access requires a research relationship with the relevant Hungarian education authority, not a public release.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: A large, nationally representative Indian household survey (the IHDS-II wave, covering over 42,000 households across more than 1,500 villages and nearly 1,000 urban neighborhoods), used in the single paper citing it here to supply the individual- and household-level microdata that India's own census cannot provide directly (see Census of India, elsewhere in this document) -- specifically training a generative model (a Conditional Tabular GAN) to produce realistic, correlated individual attributes (height, weight, comorbidities) for a large-scale synthetic population, going beyond what marginal-only census data can support on its own. As with the Census of India entry, this source shares the same underlying currency problem: the paper notes its expected successor wave (IHDS-III, expected in 2023) still had not been publicly released as of the paper's own late-2024 publication, leaving this synthetic-population effort still dependent on the 2011-12 wave of data.
accessibility_description: A large household survey; individual- and household-level microdata access requires a research agreement, not a public release.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: US tax-filing-derived county-to-county migration data, used in the single paper citing it here as one of several administrative data sources benchmarked for migration modeling. This source has the longest continuous time span of any migration data source in this document (30 consecutive yearly datasets, 1990-2020), but shares the same structural pattern as the other US administrative migration sources here: flows below a small threshold (20 individuals) are suppressed for privacy, and the overwhelming majority of possible county-pair flows (99.2%) are recorded as zero. A specific coverage gap distinguishes this source from census-based alternatives: because it is built from tax filings, it necessarily excludes anyone who does not file taxes, and provides no demographic detail about who is moving.
accessibility_description: Publicly released by the IRS at the county level; individual-level tax data is not accessible.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: Italy's national statistics agency, used across two papers here as ancillary demographic and population-density context rather than as a primary mobility source in its own right. One paper draws on detailed 2011 census building- and population-characteristic variables (building age, height, residential status, employee counts) to help characterize urban diversity across city blocks. A second paper uses Istat's official 2020 population-density projections as ground truth to validate a mobile-phone-derived population-density estimate during the COVID-19 period -- a case where official statistics serve specifically as the accuracy benchmark for a newer, commercially-derived mobility product, rather than being analyzed on their own.
accessibility_description: Publicly released national census and statistical data.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: Japan's national population census, accessed via the government's e-Stat data portal and used in the single paper citing it here in an unusual role: as the *sole input* to a migration-flow estimation model, rather than as validation ground truth for a model built from richer mobility data. Using only year-over-year population counts across Japan's 47 prefectures (2010 and 2011), the paper's radiation-model-based approach estimates underlying migration flows and is then checked against actual recorded 2010 migration data -- essentially testing how much can be inferred about movement from population change alone, without any direct mobility signal. The paper candidly notes the radiation model carries its own intrinsic error that limits how well this census-only approach can perform, even with the best-performing variant of its estimation method.
accessibility_description: Publicly accessible via Japan's official e-Stat government statistics portal.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: An open-access UK government data portal providing detailed 2011 census microdata (age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic indicators, household composition), used in the single paper citing it here to construct the demographic backbone of a large-scale synthetic population (the JUNE epidemic simulation, modeling all of England's population, roughly 53 million people, at output-area resolution). NOMIS is described directly in the citing paper as the specific access portal through which UK census microdata is provided by the Office for National Statistics -- register data keeps it as a separate entry from the 'Office for National Statistics' source elsewhere in this document, since NOMIS specifically names an access mechanism/microdata product, while the ONS entry covers a different specific data product (commuting origin-destination data) from the same underlying government agency, similar to how Telecom Italia and its mobile subsidiary TIM are kept as separate entries elsewhere in this document. Worth reconsidering together if that distinction turns out not to matter for how this document is ultimately used.
accessibility_description: An open-access UK government microdata portal, provided by the Office for National Statistics.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: A nationwide Indian household survey covering socioeconomic topics including employment, used in the single paper citing it here for a specific, narrow purpose within a larger synthetic-population pipeline (BharatSim): estimating which simulated individuals should be classified as 'homebound' (not attending work or school) based on district-level employment data, feeding downstream logic for assigning workplaces and schools elsewhere in the same synthetic population.
accessibility_description: A nationwide government household survey; district-level aggregate data used here.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description:
The UK's national statistics agency. This entry merges what were initially two separate register rows -- 'Office for National Statistics' and 'National Statistics (UK)' -- since the paper citing the latter explicitly refers to its own data as 'ONS internal migration matrices,' confirming it is the same agency under a slightly different register name, not a distinct source.

Across the three papers now grouped here, uses include supplying commuting origin-destination data to populate a large synthetic population's inter-workplace commuting structure (the same JUNE simulation that also draws on the NOMIS census-microdata portal, elsewhere in this document), providing socio-demographic area classifications used alongside land-use data in a London footfall-prediction model, and supplying internal migration matrices (2012-2019, 338 regions) used to calibrate a random-walk population-redistribution model -- that model's simulated population deviated from the real UK population by only 0.14-0.16 on average, a comparatively tight fit among the migration-modeling papers in this document. One paper notes a specific scope limit on UK migration statistics generally: they only count migrations that occurred within the preceding 12 months, meaning longer-term or more gradual relocation patterns are not captured by this kind of annual snapshot.
accessibility_description: Publicly released UK government statistics, available directly or through affiliated portals such as NOMIS.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description:
The US decennial census and its associated commuting/population products. This entry merges what were initially two separate register rows -- 'United States Census' and 'US Census (2010)' -- since both clearly refer to the same underlying institution, just with different specific census years or derived products cited across papers (2000 commuting flow data, 2010 population figures, 2011 metro-area estimates, and 2016 ZIP-code population figures all appear across the papers now grouped here).

One specific data-quality quirk recurs and is worth flagging clearly: several papers here needed county-to-county commuter flow data specifically, but the 2010 census did not collect this in the same form as the 2000 census did -- one paper states this plainly, explaining why it fell back to using 2000-vintage commuting data despite wanting more current figures, a genuine discontinuity in what this source can provide depending on exactly which census year a study needs. Applications across the eight papers now grouped here are wide-ranging: validating radiation-model and other spatial-interaction-model predictions against real county population and commuting patterns (one comparison finding a purpose-built 'two-trip' model fit real census-derived settlement-rank distributions far better than either gravity or standard radiation models), estimating an epidemic mixing parameter from state-level migration ratios, labeling census tracts by predominant racial/ethnic group for an urban-parks-access study, validating location-based-service user counts against true ZIP-code populations (finding a moderate correlation, ρ=0.73, with some ZIP codes showing very few active app users despite large real populations), and building a static county-to-county commuting network for an early-outbreak spread model.
accessibility_description: Publicly released US Census Bureau data across multiple census years and derived products; freely available.

section: Census and Government Demographic and Administrative Records
description: US Postal Service household change-of-address filings, used in the single paper citing it here (obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request) to quantify actual net household migration out of New York City into surrounding tri-state counties during the early COVID-19 period (April-June 2020), and to test whether that migration signal predicted subsequent second-wave case counts in the receiving counties -- finding a reasonably strong statistical relationship (R²=0.74). This is one of the few sources in this document capturing genuine, deliberate relocation (someone formally redirecting their mail) rather than incidental location signals, making it a comparatively direct measure of real migration, distinct from the many sources in this document that infer migration indirectly from where someone's phone or social media activity happens to concentrate. Two specific limitations are worth flagging: USPS did not provide counts below 10 household moves per month for any given area (a coarser suppression threshold than some other administrative sources), and the data reports only household counts, with no information on how many people typically belong to each moving household.
accessibility_description: Not a standing public dataset; the citing paper obtained this data via a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request.
region: United States (New York City and surrounding counties)

section: Travel and Commuting Surveys
description: A large, internationally standardized household survey program (used here for its Zambia implementation), used in the single paper citing it here as one of four distinct mobility data sources compared for measles transmission modeling -- the same study responsible for the well-known finding elsewhere in this review that outbreak-seeding predictions varied sharply depending on which of these four sources was used to parameterize the model. DHS plays a double role in that study: as an independent mobility signal in its own right (a 2018 stratified sample covering 112 of 115 districts as trip origins, though notably zero districts as recorded destinations -- a genuine, structural asymmetry in what this survey captures), and as a source of phone-ownership and internet-use statistics used to reweight and correct the other three mobility sources in the same study for coverage bias. The survey's own documented limitation is candidly stated in the source material itself: DHS surveys are 'designed to be representative,' but collected only at infrequent intervals, making them a poor fit for tracking anything that changes quickly.
accessibility_description: A large, standardized international survey program; access to detailed data for this specific research use required a research relationship, per register data.

section: Travel and Commuting Surveys
description:
An open-source mobile mapping tool, used in a rural Peruvian Amazon malaria-mobility pilot study to collect self-reported travel routes: 33 participants across six rural villages drew polylines representing their own remembered trip routes directly onto a tablet, rather than having their movement recorded automatically by any sensor. This is a genuinely unusual method among the sources in this document -- explicitly participatory and effortful (the participant has to actively reconstruct and draw each trip) rather than passive.

A methodological note on the source material itself: both documents available for this entry are peer-review commentaries on the underlying study, not the primary study paper. This means the description here is built from reviewers' summaries and critiques rather than the authors' own full account, and should be read with that in mind. Both reviewers independently flag the same core concerns: no independent validation data (such as a travel survey or GPS trace) exists to confirm the drawn routes are accurate, the recall-based, effortful nature of the method likely biases toward omitting shorter or less memorable trips, and (per one reviewer) questions about how GPS/mapping accuracy might be affected by cloud cover in this specific rural context remain unresolved.
accessibility_description: An open-source mobile data-collection tool; freely available, though the specific study data itself is a small research pilot rather than a public dataset.

dataset_name: Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) Person Trip data
section: Travel and Commuting Surveys
description: A large body of person-trip travel surveys conducted by JICA across 52 developing-world cities between 1966 and 2004 (with the 15 most recently surveyed cities' data publicly accessible), used in the single paper citing it here to reconstruct fine-grained population distributions for cities including Hanoi, Manila, and Jakarta. Raw survey coverage is genuinely substantial for a decades-old paper-based survey program -- sampling 1-6% of each city's population, with 78-84% of trips successfully route-matched after cleaning -- and the paper's core methodological contribution is correcting known survey artifacts before using this data as a spatial-population proxy: questionnaire responses cluster suspiciously around round numbers like 7:00 or 7:30 (a well-documented self-report rounding bias, corrected here via kernel density smoothing), and geocoding entire survey zones to a single centroid point creates artificial spatial sparsity, especially in large suburban zones (corrected via road-network and land-use-weighted spatial smoothing). Applying all three corrections together substantially improved agreement with an independent satellite-based population dataset in at least one city (correlation rising from 0.33 to 0.73 for Hanoi specifically), illustrating how much a decades-old travel survey's spatial usefulness depends on careful post-processing rather than the raw responses alone.
accessibility_description: Survey data collected by JICA across many developing-world cities; the 15 most recently surveyed cities' data is publicly accessible, per the citing paper, though full access terms are not detailed.

dataset_name: Japan Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism person-trip survey
section: Travel and Commuting Surveys
description: A Japanese government person-trip survey (used here for the Kanto region, including Tokyo), used in the single paper citing it here to build a proximity-based contact network -- linking individuals who were near each other in space, time, and mode of transport -- to drive an agent-based epidemic simulation. Because the raw survey only records origin and destination points rather than a continuous path between them, the paper had to interpolate the actual trip trace using GIS methods before any proximity analysis was possible. A specific, deliberate privacy design choice in the survey itself limits precision beyond what data-cleaning can recover: locations were recorded at a spatial resolution coarse enough that a respondent's exact location genuinely cannot be determined, by design, not merely due to measurement noise.
accessibility_description: A Japanese government survey; register data marks this as open.

section: Travel and Commuting Surveys
description: A US Census Bureau administrative product providing detailed commuting flow counts between census tracts, used in the single paper citing it here to build a very large national commuting network (2016 data: over 72,000 census tracts as nodes, over 26 million weighted edges) and test how much of that network can be removed while preserving realistic epidemic (SIR) simulation behavior. Using a principled network-sparsification technique (effective-resistance sampling), the paper found that keeping only 7% of edges preserved simulation dynamics well while cutting runtime by roughly 85% -- a concrete, quantified demonstration that a commuting network this large carries substantial redundant structure from an epidemic-modeling perspective, not just from a data-storage one. The paper is candid about a more fundamental limitation beyond network size, though: commute flows alone, however completely captured, are 'almost certainly too simplistic to capture the dynamics of modern epidemics,' since they omit all non-commute movement entirely.
accessibility_description: A publicly released US Census Bureau administrative data product; freely available.

section: Travel and Commuting Surveys
description: A six-week travel diary study (230 individuals, 8,522 total daily schedules), used in the single paper citing it here -- alongside two other travel-diary sources, Thurgau 2003 and the California-NHTS, all analyzed together in the same study -- to test whether individual daily activity schedules follow a Zipf-style power-law distribution. At the individual level, the paper found only a small minority of people (4%, 9 of 230) actually showed behavior statistically indistinguishable from a true power law, a much lower share than the same paper found using the larger datasets analyzed alongside it -- a finding the paper attributes at least partly to this dataset's comparatively small per-individual sample size falling below what is generally considered the minimum needed for reliable power-law testing.
accessibility_description: Access mechanism not detailed in the citing paper.

section: Travel and Commuting Surveys
description:
The US National Household Travel Survey program, including its California-specific state add-on sample, used across four papers here for genuinely varied purposes: testing power-law behavior in daily activity schedules at national scale (over 257,000 schedules from the 2009 wave), studying how older adults' daily mobility patterns differ structurally from younger populations using California's 2017 data (finding that seniors are considerably more likely to have simple, single-destination 'home loop' travel patterns than more complex multi-stop days), and validating a large-language-model-based synthetic activity-generation method against real Los Angeles-area travel-diary data as ground truth (finding close statistical agreement between the generated and real activity-chain distributions).

The power-law study is worth noting as analyzing this source alongside two much smaller travel-diary datasets in the same paper -- MobiDrive 1999 and Thurgau 2003, both described separately elsewhere in this document -- specifically to compare how power-law fit quality changes with sample size, finding this larger national dataset supports the power-law finding more robustly than either smaller diary study.
accessibility_description: A publicly released US government travel survey program, including state-level add-on samples; freely available for research use.

section: Travel and Commuting Surveys
description: A six-week travel diary study conducted in the Swiss canton of Thurgau (230 individuals, 8,522 total daily schedules -- coincidentally the same sample size reported for MobiDrive 1999, elsewhere in this document, though these are described as distinct studies), used in the single paper citing it here -- the same paper analyzing MobiDrive 1999 and California-NHTS together -- to test power-law behavior in individual daily activity schedules. As with MobiDrive, only a small minority of individuals here (4%) showed behavior statistically consistent with a true power law at the individual level, a pattern the paper attributes to the same small-sample-size limitation affecting both smaller diary datasets in its comparison.
accessibility_description: Access mechanism not detailed in the citing paper.

section: Travel and Commuting Surveys
description: A Mexico City origin-destination travel survey (2017, covering 16 boroughs), used in the single paper citing it here as the structural backbone for a COVID-19 transmission model -- the 2017 survey's mode-specific trip matrix is rebalanced day-by-day using real-time Google and government mobility-change data, rather than being used as a static, unchanging input. The paper notes a specific asymmetry worth flagging for any similar origin-destination application: the resulting matrix does not have to be, and in practice was not, symmetric (a borough that draws heavy inbound trip volume during the day is not simply the mirror image of a borough that generates them). The paper also notes candidly that no more recent ground-truth survey exists to update this 2017 baseline.
accessibility_description: A government-conducted origin-destination travel survey; publicly available.

dataset_name: Domestic Airline Fares Consumer Report (US Department of Transportation)
section: Air Travel Networks and Flight Data
description: A US Department of Transportation air-travel report, used in the single paper citing it here to build a 114-city air-travel network for an influenza spread model, drawing specifically on daily average passenger counts for the largest city-pair markets in the contiguous 48 states during the first quarter of 2011. Despite covering only 114 of the many US cities with air service, this subset is disproportionately important -- the paper reports these 114 cities alone account for roughly 75% of all domestic passenger traffic within the 48 states and 70% of total US domestic passenger traffic -- meaning a comparatively small, manageable network captures the large majority of actual air-travel volume.
accessibility_description: Publicly released by the US Department of Transportation.

section: Air Travel Networks and Flight Data
description: Brazil's civil aviation regulator, whose flight-level air-traffic statistics are used across two papers here -- one building and analyzing the complete Brazilian air-travel network across three full years (2019-2021, spanning the sharp COVID-era disruption to air travel), and a second using multi-year average passenger volume (roughly 80 million passengers annually, representing an estimated 39% of the population) as one component of a broader national mobility dataset for pathogen-surveillance-site planning.
accessibility_description: Publicly released national civil aviation statistics.

section: Air Travel Networks and Flight Data
description:
A commercial global flight-schedule data provider. This entry merges what were initially two separate register rows -- 'OAG' and 'Official Airline Guide (OAG)' -- since OAG is simply the standard abbreviation for the same company, not a distinct source.

Across the two papers now grouped here, OAG's flux data anchors two structurally different global air-mobility analyses. One builds a Markov-chain 'effective distance' measure over a large global network (3,865 airports, over 51,000 directed routes) that predicts how quickly an epidemic seeded at one airport would reach any other, finding this random-walk-based distance measure fits observed spread patterns even better than simple shortest-path distance. The other, working from an earlier (2000) snapshot of the same kind of OAG data, specifically tests how much the airport network can be downsampled while preserving realistic epidemic-simulation behavior -- finding that a carefully chosen sample of just 52 cities still captures roughly 40% of total air traffic volume, rising to 90% with 500 cities -- directly relevant to any node-reduction approach to simplifying an air-travel network for epidemic modeling. Both papers note OAG's own claimed data completeness (the company states 99% of commercial airlines report their scheduled flights) as a stated, not independently verified, coverage figure, and one paper notes explicitly that this kind of scheduled-flight data cannot capture regional connectivity that occurs mainly by ground transport rather than air, particularly around smaller airports.
accessibility_description: A commercial flight-schedule data provider; accessed through a data license, not a public dataset.

section: Air Travel Networks and Flight Data
description:
The US government's official air-travel statistics agency, whose quarterly Origin & Destination Survey (a 10% random sample of all US domestic airline passengers, running continuously since 1993) is used in the single paper citing it here to build a software tool ('AIRNET') for constructing dynamic US intercity air-transport networks over time. A single recent quarter alone (2011 Q4) contained nearly 15 million individual passenger movements across 448 airports, and the paper aggregates this down to 139 'primary hub' airports capturing over 92% of actual passenger movement, closely mirroring the same kind of small-network-captures-most-of-the-traffic pattern also seen in the Domestic Airline Fares Consumer Report elsewhere in this document.

Two structural limitations are worth flagging clearly for any epidemic-modeling application specifically. First, being restricted to US domestic flights, this source systematically biases any centrality or connectivity measure computed from it -- the paper gives a concrete example, noting Atlanta appears more central than Miami purely because Miami's substantial international air traffic is excluded from the network entirely, not because Atlanta genuinely handles more total traffic. Second, and more fundamentally, airline data of this kind systematically underestimates short-haul intercity connectivity wherever driving or rail is a viable substitute for flying -- the paper's own example finds the New York-Philadelphia air link carries only 2,180 passengers over three months, despite these being major, heavily-connected cities, because most travelers between them simply do not fly.
accessibility_description: Publicly released US government aviation statistics, based on a continuous 10% random sample of ticketed passengers since 1993.

section: Air Travel Networks and Flight Data
description: A global airport-connectivity dataset built from the OpenFlights database (2014 release: 3,458 airports connected by nearly 69,000 routes), used in the single paper citing it here to compute an 'Airport Expected Force' (AEF) metric estimating how much epidemic-spreading potential a given airport carries based purely on its local network position. This same paper (`W3103954000`) received close, direct scrutiny elsewhere in this broader review project as a possible cross-check on a proposed airport-network node-reduction strategy for GLEAM -- that examination concluded AEF does not transfer usefully to validate large-scale node reduction, both because it was only tested at a much smaller removal scale (1-15% of US airports) than a large global reduction would require, and because AEF measures a different underlying quantity (a topological summary statistic) than what a node-reduction method actually needs to preserve (disease-transmission dynamics themselves). The paper is explicit that AEF is structurally blind to certain failure cases by construction, since it only considers an airport's immediate two-hop neighborhood: it specifically breaks down for small, locally dense but poorly globally connected communities, with one particular airport (on Paama Island, Vanuatu) flagged as likely mischaracterized in the underlying OpenFlights data entirely -- a useful, concrete illustration of exactly the kind of small-node fragility this broader review's benchmark work independently identified as a general risk for airport-network simplification methods.
accessibility_description: Built from OpenFlights, a crowdsourced but not fully open-access airline route database; access terms for the specific 2014 release used here are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: Public Transit Records
description: Madrid's public bicycle-sharing system, used in the single paper citing it here to study how the system is actually used -- specifically, whether a given trip looks like genuine point-to-point transport or more leisurely, exploratory cycling. Working from one month of trip data (February 2019, roughly 304,000 raw trips), the paper compares each trip's actual path against the shortest possible route between its start and end station to classify it, finding the large majority of trips (about 91%) fall into the 'transport' category rather than leisure riding -- a directly quantified answer to a question (is this mode used mainly for utilitarian trips or recreation?) that matters for deciding how to represent bike-share in any broader mobility model.
accessibility_description: Publicly available bike-share trip data from Madrid's public bicycle-sharing operator.

section: Public Transit Records
description: Barcelona's public bicycle-sharing system, used in the single paper citing it here in an unusual way: rather than accessing official trip records directly, the researchers mined a publicly accessible real-time station-status feed (a KML file the system published showing bikes and free slots per station, updated every two minutes) over seven weeks in 2008, and inferred likely origin-destination trip patterns indirectly from the resulting pattern of stations emptying and filling over time, using a maximum-entropy model rather than working from any ground-truth trip record at all. The paper is candid that this indirect, web-scraped signal is 'in principle very noisy,' and that station-count patterns are further complicated by the system's own rebalancing trucks moving bikes between stations, which can look like genuine user activity if not accounted for. Data collection itself broke down partway through the study window, forcing the analysis to use a shorter period than originally planned.
accessibility_description: Mined from a publicly accessible real-time station-status feed published by the Bicing system; not an official trip-record release.

section: Public Transit Records
description: An open data project documenting Nairobi's semi-formal 'matatu' minibus transit system, used in the single paper citing it here (the project's own foundational paper) to describe how route and schedule data for an informal transit network -- one that has no official, reliable government documentation to begin with -- can be collected and published in a standard, reusable format. A small team physically rode or followed matatus across Nairobi's more than 135 routes over roughly six months to record actual route paths and stop locations, motivated specifically because existing government route records (kept as basic word-processing documents) were found to be 'incomplete, outdated, and inaccurate.' A genuine methodological challenge specific to this kind of informal transit system is documented directly: routes themselves are not fixed, and shift due to road construction, drivers avoiding police checkpoints, or school schedules, requiring repeated resurveying to settle on each route's 'most consistent' path rather than a single, stable ground truth. The resulting data was converted into a modified version of the standard GTFS transit-data format (adapted for this kind of semi-formal system) and released openly.
accessibility_description: Openly released via GTFS Exchange, following field data collection specifically because no reliable official transit data existed for this system.

section: Public Transit Records
description:
A standardized, open data format for describing public transit routes and schedules (not itself a single dataset, but a shared specification that many transit agencies publish their own data in). This entry merges what were initially two separate register rows -- 'GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification)' and 'General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS)' -- since these simply describe the same standard with the acronym expansion written in a different order, not two different formats or datasets.

The two papers now grouped here use GTFS-formatted transit schedules for genuinely different cities and purposes: one combines Santiago, Chile's bus-route GTFS feed with road-network data to label mobile-phone cell towers by likely nearby transport mode (distinguishing car-adjacent from bus-corridor-adjacent towers), feeding a model that infers commute mode from network signaling data alone. The other uses Tallinn, Estonia's GTFS feed directly to model how accessible different parts of the city are by public transit plus walking, recalculated across the day to capture how service frequency changes accessibility over time. That second paper documents a specific, quantified limitation worth flagging for any GTFS-based accessibility modeling generally: because GTFS describes *planned* schedules rather than what vehicles actually did, accessibility estimates built from it overestimate real-world accessibility by roughly 4-15%, since real service delays and disruptions are invisible to the schedule data.
accessibility_description: An open, standardized data format; individual transit agencies publish their own GTFS feeds freely, though data completeness and update frequency vary by agency.

section: Public Transit Records
description: London's metro system, whose automated fare collection (AFC) records -- tap-in/tap-out tuples of traveler, origin/destination station, and entry/exit time -- are used in the single paper citing it here to build personalized trip-time prediction models from individual travelers' own historical patterns. Two separate 83-day samples (each a 5% subsample of all riders, roughly 300,000 travelers apiece) reveal a striking behavioral regularity worth noting on its own: roughly 60% of user-trip pairs are genuine repeat trips by the same day-83 mark, and the large majority of riders (88%+) complete a same-day round trip (a loop back to somewhere near where they started) -- a strong, directly measured instance of the routine, repetitive movement pattern assumed by many mobility models generally. The paper is explicit that its own models deliberately exclude several richer data sources that could improve prediction further -- network topology, train schedules, service disruptions, and transfer information -- meaning the reported results likely understate what this kind of transit-card data could support with fuller access.
accessibility_description: Automated fare-collection transaction data; not a public dataset, made available for this specific research use as a 5% anonymized subsample.

section: Public Transit Records
description: Montreal's public transit smart-card system, used in the single paper citing it here to study how individual transit riders' usage patterns vary over an entire year (429 million card validations from roughly 2 million cards in 2016) -- a genuinely large-scale, individual-level, longitudinal dataset by the standards of this document. The paper builds four indicators specifically to characterize ridership variability (how spread-out a rider's trips are, how variable their travel frequency is month to month, and how spatially diverse their boarding locations are), and uses inequality-curve analysis to show trip counts are highly concentrated among a minority of frequent riders -- the same kind of Pareto-style usage skew documented for several other transit and check-in sources in this document. A specific, structural limitation is worth flagging clearly: the unit of analysis here is the *card*, not the person -- an anonymous card can be shared among multiple people, and conversely one person may hold more than one card, meaning card-level statistics do not translate cleanly into individual-level ridership figures.
accessibility_description: Smart-card transaction data from Montreal's transit authority (STM); not a public dataset, made available for this specific research use.

section: Public Transit Records
description: The University at Buffalo's campus smart-card system, used in the single paper citing it here to reconstruct detailed daily activity-and-movement sequences for a small sample of students (37 students, over five consecutive days, from over 1,400 recorded swipe transactions across 11 facility categories -- dining halls, libraries, gyms, and similar). This is a genuinely fine-grained, campus-scale mobility source distinct from the city- or national-scale transit-card sources elsewhere in this document. The paper's own reconstructed-schedule accuracy improves meaningfully when incorporating a student's own established weekly pattern (e.g., using their known Monday/Tuesday class schedule to infer likely gaps later in the week) rather than relying on swipe records alone. Two coverage gaps are worth flagging plainly: recreational activities are substantially under-captured (by roughly 56%) since they only appear in the data when a swipe-required facility happens to be used, and purely social or event-based participation is invisible to this data entirely (0% coverage), since no swipe is required to attend.
accessibility_description: Campus smart-card transaction data; not a public dataset, made available for this specific research use.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: A Paris hospital's intensive-care admission records, used in the single paper citing it here to derive age-stratified clinical severity parameters (586 ICU patients, March 2020-January 2021) for a COVID-19 compartmental model -- specifically, the age-dependent infection fatality ratio, which the paper finds rises sharply with age (from roughly 0.0005% in the youngest bracket to 2.67% in the oldest, a more than 5,000-fold range). The paper is explicit about a real generalizability limit: parameters derived from a single Paris hospital's patient population were then applied as a national-level template, and the smallest age bracket (0-19) had no usable data at all, requiring the paper to fill that gap some other way rather than from this source directly.
accessibility_description: Anonymized clinical hospitalization data from a single hospital; not a public dataset.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: Brazil's national disease-notification system, whose weekly city-level dengue incidence records are used in the single paper citing it here to jointly estimate both a mobility rate and transmission parameters for a two-city, mobility-coupled dengue model, across four Rio de Janeiro state cities of substantially different size (from roughly 218,000 to 855,000 residents). A methodological limitation the paper flags directly is worth generalizing: several fitted mobility-rate estimates converged to the upper bound the researchers had imposed on the model, rather than settling on an internally-determined value -- a sign the underlying fitting problem is, in the paper's own words, 'ill-posed,' with initial conditions alone capable of shifting the resulting parameter estimates.
accessibility_description: Publicly released Brazilian government disease-surveillance data.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, whose COVID-19 vaccine rollout data (Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna distribution/administration figures) is used in the single paper citing it here to fit a vaccination-adoption curve (finding roughly 5.4% of the population fully vaccinated by February 20, 2021) feeding into a broader epidemic model spanning 381 US metropolitan statistical areas.
accessibility_description: Publicly released US government vaccination data.

dataset_name: CDC Wide-Ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER)
section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: A CDC public health data query system, used in the single paper citing it here to collect county-level opioid overdose death counts (identified via standard diagnostic codes) as the calibration target for a two-level model of the opioid crisis across 67 Pennsylvania counties, with Philadelphia showing the highest baseline overdose rate among the counties studied. The same paper here also draws on IQVIA's prescription-dispensing data (see the IQVIA entry elsewhere in this document) as a companion input, using this CDC source specifically for the outcome being modeled rather than the underlying driver.
accessibility_description: A public, freely queryable CDC data system.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: A large UK household survey combining serological (antibody) testing with self-reported infection data, contributing to a combined dataset of nearly 9,000 observations (alongside population, case, death, and hospital-admission figures) used in the single paper citing it here to fit a detailed, 150-plus-parameter age-stratified COVID-19 model -- including estimating that roughly 55% of infections were asymptomatic overall. This survey plays an outsized, load-bearing role for one specific age group: for the 80-and-older bracket, the paper notes this survey is the *sole* source of information determining the asymptomatic-branching probability estimate, and flags a genuine ambiguity in interpreting its own data for that group -- the low antibody-positivity rate observed near the end of 2020 could reflect either genuinely low exposure in that age group, or antibody levels waning faster than expected, or simply false-negative test results, and the survey data alone cannot distinguish between these explanations.
accessibility_description: Publicly released UK survey data.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
