description: Clinical COVID-19 case and hospitalization data for Switzerland, compiled by ETH Zurich, used in the single paper citing it here to fit a simpler, homogeneous-mixing SEIR model first, whose fitted parameters then seed a more detailed geospatial stochastic simulation for Geneva -- a two-stage approach where this data source's role is specifically to provide a reasonable starting point for the more complex model, not to calibrate it directly end-to-end. The paper's fitted transmission rate shifts sharply across five distinct regimes over the modeled period, tracking major policy or behavioral changes rather than remaining constant.
accessibility_description: Compiled by ETH Zurich; exact access terms are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: The World Health Organization's global influenza surveillance platform, used in the single paper citing it here to validate a combined GLEAM-metapopulation and phylogeographic model of global influenza circulation. The validation result is itself informative about a broader pattern relevant to global epidemic surveillance generally: agreement between the simulated and FluNet-observed epidemic timing was strong in the Northern Hemisphere (correlation 0.83) but weakened substantially moving toward the equator, becoming essentially uninformative in tropical regions (correlation only 0.10) -- the paper attributes this directly to genuinely noisier, flatter surveillance signal in tropical countries and to large countries spanning enough climatic variation internally that a single national-level FluNet time series can obscure real sub-national spatial structure.
accessibility_description: Publicly released WHO global surveillance data.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: The primary global repository for shared SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequences, used in the single paper citing it here to estimate daily international variant-importation counts from sequence metadata (collection date, country, and lineage) alone, across over 2 million sequences submitted by mid-2022. The paper's central limitation is a genuine, quantified representativeness problem directly relevant to any global genomic-surveillance application: sequencing capacity is heavily concentrated in a small number of well-resourced countries (the US and UK alone contributed nearly 55% of all sequences, and just 10% of countries produced over 90% of the total), meaning variant detection and importation estimates are systematically better resolved for some countries than others, independent of actual epidemiological importance.
accessibility_description: A global genomic data-sharing platform; access requires registration and agreement to GISAID's data-sharing terms.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: A commercial healthcare-data analytics company, whose monthly county-level prescription-dispensing rates (for opioids, naloxone, and buprenorphine) are used in the single paper citing it here -- the same opioid-crisis study also drawing on CDC WONDER data (see elsewhere in this document) -- as the intervention-level input feeding a response-function model of overdose outcomes. The paper is direct that this specific data is not publicly available at all, requiring a formal request through the IQVIA Institute rather than any open access route.
accessibility_description: A commercial healthcare-data product; not publicly available, requires a formal request through the IQVIA Institute.

dataset_name: Johns Hopkins University COVID-19 Dataset (JHU CSSE)
section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description:
The Johns Hopkins University Center for Systems Science and Engineering's COVID-19 data repository -- among the most widely used pandemic data sources in the world, and one of the most-cited sources in this document. This entry merges what were initially two separate register rows -- 'Johns Hopkins University COVID-19 dataset' and 'Johns Hopkins University Center for Systems Science and Engineering (JHU CSSE)' -- since both names refer interchangeably to the exact same underlying data repository, commonly called by either name in the literature.

Across the five papers now grouped here, uses range from providing daily national case/recovery/death counts as ground truth for automated parameter extraction and hardware-accelerated Bayesian model fitting, to supplying county-level case and testing data aggregated to 381 US metropolitan statistical areas for a vaccination-and-intervention outcome study, to serving as the target series for a top-performing real-time Bayesian mortality forecasting model (ranked in the top two of ten models in an official US COVID-19 Forecast Hub comparison). Two papers directly address the same well-known limitation of this kind of confirmed-case data: one estimates the true US infection count was 20-30% higher than what was ever officially reported as a confirmed case, and another documents specific, large single-day reporting anomalies requiring manual correction (a one-day backlog addition of 1,600 deaths in New Jersey; a one-day subtraction of 3,000 cases in Texas) -- concrete illustrations that even a widely-trusted, continuously-updated case-count feed can contain sharp, non-epidemiological artifacts that a naive model-fitting process would otherwise treat as real signal.
accessibility_description: Freely and publicly released by Johns Hopkins University, updated continuously throughout the pandemic; no registration or agreement required.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: A synthetic Ebola outbreak dataset (built from a high-resolution agent-based simulator, released for a formal forecasting challenge as part of the RAPIDD/NIH Ebola Forecasting Challenge, with a synthetic Liberia scenario released incrementally at five successive time points), used in the single paper citing it here to validate a novel particle-filtering method against simpler phenomenological baseline models. The paper's own proposed method substantially outperformed the baselines at the earliest checkpoints tested (correlation 0.80 and 0.94 at the first two release points, versus baseline correlations as poor as -0.79, i.e., actively wrong-direction), illustrating this challenge dataset's intended purpose well: providing a controlled, common ground truth specifically to compare competing forecasting methods' early-outbreak performance, when real data is by nature most limited and hardest to forecast from.
accessibility_description: Released publicly as part of a formal, NSF/NIH-sponsored forecasting challenge.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: An open global dengue-surveillance database, used in the single paper citing it here to retrieve 13 years of weekly, municipality-level Colombian dengue incidence data (over 163,000 records across 211 municipalities) to calibrate a Gaussian-Process emulator standing in for a more expensive individual-based dengue transmission model. The paper applies a substantial correction factor (multiplying raw reported incidence by 25) to account for known dengue under-reporting -- a specific, quantified illustration of how large a gap can exist between officially reported and true disease incidence for a condition like dengue, where many cases go undiagnosed or unreported. The paper also notes a mobility-specific limitation directly relevant to this broader document: no fine-scale mobility data was available for this application at all, forcing the authors to substitute a much coarser mean-travel-time proxy in its place.
accessibility_description: A publicly accessible, open global disease-surveillance database.

dataset_name: The New York Times COVID-19 data
section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: A widely used, journalist-compiled COVID-19 case and death tracking dataset, used in the single paper citing it here as the observation series for calibrating a stochastic SEIRD compartmental model for Philadelphia, split into a training window (July-October 2020) and a held-out test window (October-November 2020) to evaluate real forecasting performance rather than only fit quality.
accessibility_description: Freely and publicly released, updated daily throughout the pandemic.

section: Epidemiological and Disease Surveillance Data
description: The WHO's own outbreak case-reporting records, used across two papers here for epidemic-potential and spatial-spread analysis of two different diseases. One paper uses WHO H5N1 (avian influenza) case counts from Vietnam and Indonesia in a Bayesian framework to bound how far a small number of observed human-to-human clusters could push an estimate of the disease's sustained-transmission potential, explicitly noting that surveillance data 'in these circumstances tend to be very stochastic, involve small case numbers,' and suffer from inconsistent reporting -- genuine constraints on how confidently any epidemic-potential estimate can be drawn from rare-event outbreak surveillance. A second paper uses WHO's documented but unsequenced Ebola case locations (21,811 date-location pairs) specifically to fill a gap that genomic data alone cannot: because typically only a small single-digit percentage of confirmed viral cases are ever genetically sequenced, this WHO case-location data is used to supplement a much smaller sequenced-case dataset in a combined phylogenetic-plus-spatial model of the outbreak's spread.
accessibility_description: Publicly released WHO outbreak surveillance data.

section: Contact-Pattern Surveys
description: A contact-pattern survey specifically designed to capture how social mixing changed once COVID-19 lockdown measures took effect, used in the single paper citing it here as a direct replacement for the older POLYMOD contact matrix (see elsewhere in this document) partway through an England-focused age-structured epidemic model. This substitution -- swapping in a lockdown-era contact survey specifically because the pre-pandemic POLYMOD data no longer reflected how people were actually interacting -- is a direct, applied instance of exactly the concern raised elsewhere in this document's companion review about treating contact or mobility patterns as constant through a period of behavioral disruption.
accessibility_description: Publicly released contact-survey data.

section: Contact-Pattern Surveys
description: A 2024 US contact-pattern survey (a two-wave, nationally representative panel of 1,930 respondents run through a probability-based online panel), used in the single paper citing it here -- the survey's own foundational paper -- to construct age- and setting-stratified social contact matrices for modeling respiratory pathogen spread. The survey found an average of 7.4 contacts per person per day, and its results correlate strongly with two well-established prior contact-matrix sources (r=0.92 against one, r=0.88 against another), a reassuring sign of consistency with earlier contact-pattern research despite being a newer, differently-constructed survey. The paper is direct about two limitations: contact-diary data of this kind is subject to the respondent's own memory and recall accuracy, and the survey's sample size, while nationally representative overall, is not large enough to support reliable state-by-state breakdowns.
accessibility_description: A recent (2024) probability-based panel survey; specific data-access terms for other researchers are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: Contact-Pattern Surveys
description: A series of small-scale wireless proximity-sensing experiments (using short-range 'iMote' Bluetooth-style devices carried by participants), used in the single paper citing it here to characterize the statistical structure of human encounter patterns across five separate deployments -- ranging from a 3-day, 12-device pilot at Cambridge to a much larger, 98-device, 3-day deployment at the Infocom 2006 conference recording over 191,000 individual contact events. Contact rates vary dramatically across these deployments (from roughly 0.08 contacts per device-pair per day in one Hong Kong dataset to nearly 7 per pair per day at the Infocom conference setting), and intercontact times follow a heavy-tailed distribution whose exact shape (a fitted power-law exponent) differs meaningfully between deployment settings. Two specific limitations recur: information about contacts shorter than the device's own scanning interval (2-5 minutes) is 'irretrievably lost,' and the paper notes plainly that a device is 'not necessarily co-located with [its] owner at all times' -- a real device-versus-person distinction relevant to any proximity-sensing contact study.
accessibility_description: A well-known, openly released academic proximity-sensing dataset series.

section: Contact-Pattern Surveys
description: A landmark, multi-country European contact-pattern survey, and one of the most-cited contact-matrix sources in epidemic modeling generally -- widely reused in this literature not directly, but via a later extension (Prem et al.) that mathematically projected POLYMOD's original European survey results onto age-contact matrices for 152 countries worldwide, letting studies far beyond POLYMOD's original European scope borrow its underlying contact structure. Both papers citing it here use this extended, 152-country version rather than the original raw survey data -- one to sample plausible contact ages within a Geneva-focused stochastic epidemic simulation, the other as the *pre-lockdown baseline* contact matrix in an England-focused model, later replaced by the lockdown-specific CoMix survey once restrictions began (see the CoMix entry elsewhere in this document for that direct substitution).
accessibility_description: A well-known, openly released academic contact-survey dataset, with a widely-used global extension (Prem et al.) also freely available.

section: Contact-Pattern Surveys
description: An open collection of real-world, sensor-recorded face-to-face contact networks from specific settings, used in the single paper citing it here as realistic test substrates (specifically a 2013 high-school and a 2015 workplace network) for evaluating a fast approximate epidemic-simulation method (dynamic message passing) against full Monte Carlo simulation. The paper's own finding is a useful, general caution for anyone using a network-approximation method on real (rather than synthetic, random) contact structure: the approximation's accuracy degraded specifically on the high-school network, because that real network's structure is more tightly clustered into a few distinct communities than the approximation method assumes -- a concrete illustration that a method validated on one real network's structure may not transfer cleanly to another, even within the same general category of 'realistic human contact network.'
accessibility_description: A well-known, openly released academic collection of real-world contact-network datasets.

section: Indoor Positioning, WiFi, and Bluetooth Sensing
description: The widely-used international academic WiFi roaming network, used in the single paper citing it here to analyze a full year (2011) of connection logs from a single university's network (University of Minho, Portugal) -- nearly 16 million individual connection records -- to study human mobility at an unusually fine spatial scale (building-to-building and access-point-to-access-point movement within a campus, rather than city- or region-scale movement). Rather than using raw physical distance, the paper builds a *topological* distance measure based on how often people actually move between two access points, and finds the resulting mobility pattern is close to a simple random-walk (Brownian) process at this fine scale -- a genuinely different finding from the more structured, non-random mobility patterns typically reported at city or regional scale elsewhere in this document, suggesting mobility structure may look qualitatively different depending on the spatial scale being examined.
accessibility_description: Institutional WiFi connection logs; access requires a research relationship with the hosting university's network administration, not a public dataset.

section: Indoor Positioning, WiFi, and Bluetooth Sensing
description: A large sports and entertainment venue in Amsterdam, whose dense in-house WiFi sensor network (591 access points) is used in the single paper citing it here to track pedestrian movement during two contrasting large-crowd events -- a football match and a dance/electronic-music event -- comparing how visitors' movement behavior differs by event type. After filtering, several hundred devices per event were tracked at a coarse (10-second) time resolution, using signal-strength-based proximity detection combined with a movement-classification model that distinguishes 'moving' from 'waiting' crowd behavior. The paper is candid about a real limitation shared with other WiFi-based indoor-tracking methods: it states outright that 'the accuracy of the proximity detection method is low,' and that crowd noise causes devices to switch erratically between nearby access points in a way that requires deliberate smoothing before the resulting trajectories are usable.
accessibility_description: A venue-deployed commercial WiFi sensor network; access requires a research relationship with the venue operator, not a public dataset.

section: Indoor Positioning, WiFi, and Bluetooth Sensing
description: A large-scale campus WiFi and smartphone-sensing infrastructure (nearly 2,800 access points across a 4.4 km² campus of roughly 45,000 students and 12,000 staff), used in the single paper citing it here -- the infrastructure's own foundational paper -- to study fine-grained student mobility and social behavior over an 11-week period. This is among the most methodologically thorough indoor-positioning validations in this document: the paper reports a specific technique (fusing standard WiFi association logs with additional 'rogue' and probe-request signal readings) that increased usable location-coverage time by 71%, and validated its location-inference accuracy directly against manual observation logs, achieving 84.5-92.0% pause-detection accuracy depending on method. The paper states plainly, as a general lesson for any WiFi-association-based mobility study, that 'the raw AP association trace alone is a bad estimator of device location and mobility' due to devices erratically switching between nearby access points -- precisely the same effect flagged independently in the Johan Cruijff ArenA entry elsewhere in this document, now confirmed as a general, recurring WiFi-sensing artifact rather than a one-off issue. A further specific limitation: the paper attempted to detect MAC address randomization (a privacy feature on modern smartphones that can break device-tracking continuity), but reliably identified only 486 of over 209,000 observed MAC addresses as randomized, suggesting this kind of privacy protection may be substantially under-detected by standard methods.
accessibility_description: Campus WiFi and smartphone-sensing infrastructure; not a public dataset, access requires a research relationship with the hosting institution.

section: Indoor Positioning, WiFi, and Bluetooth Sensing
description: A Bluetooth-based indoor positioning technology (Apple's iBeacon standard), used in the single paper citing it here as the underlying hardware layer (10 battery-operated beacon units in a test laboratory corridor) feeding a broader indoor navigation and mobility-graph system, alongside the indoo.rs Navigation software described separately elsewhere in this document -- these are kept as two distinct entries since iBeacon is the positioning hardware/technology while indoo.rs is the navigation software system built on top of it, not the same thing under two names. The paper documents a specific, structural limitation of this kind of beacon-based positioning: the system 'is unable to resolve features along the short traverse axis' in long, narrow spaces (like corridors) unless additional geometric constraints are added -- beacon signal strength alone cannot distinguish position reliably in the direction perpendicular to a narrow hallway's length.
accessibility_description: A proprietary Bluetooth positioning technology; deployed here as test hardware, not a public dataset.

section: Indoor Positioning, WiFi, and Bluetooth Sensing
description: A commercial indoor-navigation software system, used in the single paper citing it here as the system under validation, combining iBeacon-based signal fingerprinting (see the iBeacon entry elsewhere in this document, from the same underlying study) with pedestrian dead-reckoning, a Kalman filter, and a higher-level geometric constraint model to improve indoor positioning along known walkable paths. The paper reports the resulting system achieves typical localization accuracy of 2-10 meters, which it describes as 'fully sufficient for many indoor navigation tasks' -- though the same underlying directional-resolution weakness documented for iBeacon (poor accuracy across the short axis of a narrow corridor) persists in this combined system as well, since it stems from the beacon hardware layer rather than the navigation software built on top of it.
accessibility_description: A commercial indoor-navigation software system; deployed here as the system under test, not a public dataset.

dataset_name: Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning land-use inventory
section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: A regional planning agency's detailed 2010 land-use inventory for the Chicago area, used in the single paper citing it here to characterize what kind of place each geotagged tweet was posted from -- spatially matching each tweet to its nearest land-use polygon (with tweets that happened to fall on road segments reassigned to the nearest actual polygon), then simplifying the inventory's original 23 fine-grained land-use classes down to 7 broader categories for analysis.
accessibility_description: Publicly released regional planning agency data.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: A UK academic geospatial data-access service (via EDINA), used in the single paper citing it here to obtain land-use classification data (a September 2021 release, aggregated into 10 land-use types per Output Area) as a spatial covariate for a Greater London human-activity study, sourced specifically from the 'UKLand' component of Digimap's commercial 'Verisk' data section.
accessibility_description: A UK academic data-access portal; the specific UKLand/Verisk data requires an institutional subscription, not open public access.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: A global satellite-derived population-density raster (part of the European Commission's Global Human Settlement Layer program), used in the single paper citing it here purely as spatial infrastructure -- building a distance matrix and weighting how likely two locations are to have contact proportional to local population density, feeding a Geneva-focused stochastic epidemic simulation. Like the geographic-reference sources elsewhere in this document, its role is providing background spatial structure rather than any movement signal itself.
accessibility_description: Publicly released global population-density raster data.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: Google's mapping platform, used in the single paper citing it here to build a large-scale park inventory (over 200,000 parks extracted across 496 urban areas in six countries) and measure walking-time-based inequality in park access, combining park location data with the platform's own Directions API and independent WorldPop population data. The paper explicitly evaluates the platform's own data quality rather than assuming it: an estimated 90% of listings were found to be spatially accurate, though outright fake listings, while rare overall (0.5% of all listings), were found concentrated specifically in the US and India (accounting for roughly 70% of all fake listings found). The paper is candid about a real structural bias beyond listing accuracy: coverage completeness itself varies meaningfully by country, and is generally biased toward higher-population-density areas, meaning sparser regions are less reliably represented regardless of listing accuracy.
accessibility_description: Accessed via Google's commercial Maps/Search/Directions APIs; requires an API license, not freely open.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: Google's points-of-interest database (queried via Google Place), used in the single paper citing it here to classify land use across Bangkok -- roughly 75,000 points of interest, aggregated to 180-meter grid cells, combined with supplementary OpenStreetMap layers for education/religious/transport categories -- specifically to characterize what kind of activity was likely happening at locations identified from geolocated tweets elsewhere in the same study. The paper is candid about a genuine sensitivity concern worth generalizing to any similar POI-based land-use classification: results 'may depend on the size/shape of the spatial aggregation unit used,' and the paper notes plainly that 'Google is not the only provider of Points of Interest' -- a different provider (Foursquare, Facebook) could plausibly yield a different land-use classification for the same city.
accessibility_description: Accessed via Google's commercial Place API; requires an API license, not freely open.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: Google's search-volume data products (Google Trends and the now-discontinued Google Flu Trends), used in the single paper citing it here as a secondary, complementary signal alongside clinical case counts for outbreak monitoring during a Canadian H1N1 wave. The paper is unusually direct about this source's limitations relative to social-media-based alternatives: search-volume data offers only daily or weekly temporal resolution and coarse geographic resolution, is 'affected by many unobserved confounders' (anything that drives search interest besides actual illness), and gives 'little sense of count of distinct users and no sense of longitudinal progression of a single user' -- explicitly describing it as comparing 'unfavourably to the richness of information' available from a source like Twitter.
accessibility_description: Accessed via Google's search-trends products; access terms and continuity vary (Google Flu Trends specifically has since been discontinued).

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: Google's street-level panoramic imagery service, used in a genuinely novel way in the single paper citing it here: manually annotating road-user counts (pedestrians, cyclists, cars, buses) visible in historical GSV panoramas across 34 Great Britain cities (68,000 raw images sampled) to predict city-level active-travel and commuting-mode shares, without any direct trip or trajectory data at all. Predictive accuracy varied sharply by mode: cycling predictions correlated strongly with independently measured cycle-commute share (r=0.92) and general past-month cycling rates (r=0.90), while car-image counts showed essentially no relationship with car commute share (r=-0.12) and walking predictions performed weakly overall. Two specific, structural limitations are worth flagging: GSV provides no metadata on exactly what time of day or day of week a given panorama was captured, and because Street View imagery is not captured in the rain, active-travel estimates built from it may be systematically biased toward fair-weather behavior.
accessibility_description: Accessed via Google's Street View imagery; requires an API license for programmatic access, though imagery itself is viewable through the standard consumer product.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: Google's public search-interest tool, used in the single paper citing it here for a narrow, specific purpose: tracking search volume for the term 'face mask' as a proxy for public awareness of mask-wearing across US metropolitan statistical areas, combined with an independent YouGov survey measure of the same underlying construct as part of a broader COVID-19 intervention-effect model.
accessibility_description: Freely and publicly accessible without registration.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: A global gridded population-density dataset, used in the single paper citing it here as pure spatial infrastructure for a large-scale synthetic population framework (BharatSim): population counts on a 1km grid are used to place synthetic individuals geographically, sampling grid cells with probability weighted by their population count and adding random jitter, to assign realistic home, workplace, school, and public-place locations. The paper is explicit about a real gap this source cannot fill on its own: with no separate workplace-density data available, workplace locations are assumed to follow the same population-density distribution as residences -- a simplifying assumption the underlying data itself cannot verify or improve on.
accessibility_description: Publicly released global gridded population data.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: A satellite-derived global population-density imagery product, used in the single paper citing it here as one of three combined inputs (alongside survey data and demographic data borrowed from a neighboring country as a proxy) for geographically placing individuals within a large synthetic Liberian population underlying an agent-based Ebola model. This synthetic population was itself later used to generate 10,000 simulated epidemic trajectories for model calibration -- illustrating how a single geographic-reference input like LandScan can end up indirectly shaping a very large downstream simulation exercise, well beyond its own direct role of simply placing people in space.
accessibility_description: A commercial/restricted satellite-derived population dataset; access terms for this specific research use are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: A European Commission land-cover and land-use mapping program for major urban areas, used in the single paper citing it here as a built-environment feature layer supporting an urban-diversity/vitality analysis of Italian cities, classifying land cover into 20 categories at sub-hectare precision with over 80% mapping accuracy. The paper notes a specific reproducibility constraint worth flagging generally: because this study also relies on mobile-phone call-record data (see the Telecom Italia entry elsewhere in this document) that cannot be shared, the paper states plainly that 'it would be difficult to fully replicate this study' even though Urban Atlas itself is openly available -- a reminder that open geographic-reference data alone does not guarantee a study's reproducibility if it is combined with restricted data elsewhere in the same analysis.
accessibility_description: Publicly released by the European Commission for major European urban areas.

section: Land Use, Built Environment, and Geographic Reference Data
description: The real-estate platform Zillow's open-source neighborhood-scale road-network dataset, used in the single paper citing it here as the empirical case-study foundation for an agent-based pedestrian-network simulation -- evaluating 708 of 16,570 available US neighborhood road networks to rank how 'permeable' (walkable, well-connected) each one is for pedestrians, and testing how much adding optimal new walking shortcuts ('desire paths') could shorten typical walking distances (finding an average reduction from 43 to 31 meters across the networks tested). This is a structural/built-environment source rather than a source of any actual movement or presence data, similar in role to the other geographic-reference sources in this document.
accessibility_description: An open-source road-network dataset released by Zillow; freely available.

section: Benchmark and Reference Trajectory or Network Datasets
description:
A large archive of physics publications, repurposed in the two papers citing it here not to study anything about physics itself, but to reconstruct individual researchers' career mobility -- treating each researcher's sequence of paper affiliations over their career (1955-2009) as a kind of trajectory, similar in spirit to the geographic mobility traces elsewhere in this document, but tracking institutional and international movement between universities and countries instead of physical location. Both papers report substantially the same findings from what appears to be the same underlying study (a raw corpus of several hundred thousand papers, narrowed after affiliation-disambiguation to just over 71,000 uniquely identified researchers across 2,434 universities and 174 countries) -- worth noting these are likely two versions of one research effort (e.g. a preprint and its published form) rather than two independent studies corroborating each other's specific figures.

The core finding, consistent across both, is that most researchers' careers show surprisingly little institutional mobility: over 40% of reconstructed career paths involve only a single affiliation ever, and 90% of researchers worked at four or fewer universities and three or fewer countries across their entire recorded career, with career location generally stabilizing after roughly six and a half years. Both papers are explicit about the same real generalizability limit: this dataset, by construction, only reflects the physics research community specifically, and cannot speak to career-mobility patterns in other academic fields.
accessibility_description: A large academic publication archive; specific access terms for bulk affiliation-history reconstruction are not detailed in either citing paper.

section: Benchmark and Reference Trajectory or Network Datasets
description: A well-known public archive of wireless-network mobility traces, used in the single paper citing it here to train and test a WiFi-access-point-based next-location prediction model (comparing a location-embedding neural network approach against simpler Markov-chain baselines). The paper's role for this source is purely as a convenient, already-public benchmark trace, rather than a source of any substantive mobility finding in its own right.
accessibility_description: A well-known, openly released academic wireless-trace archive.

section: Benchmark and Reference Trajectory or Network Datasets
description: A Meta (Facebook) 'Data for Good' product estimating how often two people from different geographic regions are likely to be physically near each other, built from opted-in Location History and Background Location data. Used across two papers here for genuinely different purposes: one is a methodological deep-dive specifically examining this product's own built-in assumptions about population representativeness and contact heterogeneity (covering all 3,142 US counties), finding opt-in adoption is itself quite low (a median of only 5.2% of the population per region) and documenting a specific, counterintuitive finding worth flagging directly: two regions can show high measured colocation 'despite few people moving' between them, since the measure captures co-presence generally, not necessarily two-way travel between the specific pair of regions. The second paper uses this same product much more directly -- as the actual parameter source for the spatial mixing structure of a simulated respiratory-pathogen model in Spain, seeded in Madrid -- illustrating a real range in how deeply a single data product can be examined versus simply plugged into a model.
accessibility_description: A Meta Data for Good product; access requires an approved research partnership, not public availability.

section: Benchmark and Reference Trajectory or Network Datasets
description: A campus-scale WiFi mobility trace dataset (566 wireless access points across 188 buildings, spanning 160 days in 2002), used in the single paper citing it here to benchmark a second-order Markov-chain path-prediction model against a standard first-order baseline. The improvement was substantial and clearly demonstrated for at least one heavily-tracked test individual: prediction accuracy roughly doubled (from 31.25% to 62.5%) when the model was allowed to condition on the previous two locations visited rather than just the most recent one.
accessibility_description: A campus WiFi trace dataset; access terms for other researchers are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: Benchmark and Reference Trajectory or Network Datasets
description: A well-known public taxi-trip GPS dataset from Porto, Portugal (1.7 million trip records from 442 taxis over one year, sampled every 15 seconds, originally released for a formal academic prediction competition), used in the single paper citing it here to benchmark a next-destination-prediction model combining trajectory clustering with an LSTM neural network and learned zone embeddings -- reporting improved accuracy over the original competition's winning approach, though noting the specific competition test set used for this comparison was quite small (only 300 trips), limiting how much weight should be placed on this exact improvement margin.
accessibility_description: A well-known, openly released academic taxi-trajectory dataset, originally published for a formal data-mining competition.

section: Benchmark and Reference Trajectory or Network Datasets
description: The European Union's flagship student exchange program, used in the single paper citing it here to build a network of student mobility and institutional cooperation spanning the large majority (90%) of European universities -- by 2014, the program had involved 3.3 million students across 4,000 institutions in 34 countries. The paper combines a gravity-model analysis of student flows with a core-periphery network structure analysis, treating student exchange itself as a form of measurable international mobility, distinct from tourism, migration, or commuting elsewhere in this document. The paper notes a specific scope limitation: its own analysis is restricted to the openly available 2007-2013 data window, not the program's full history.
accessibility_description: EU program administrative data; the specific 2007-2013 window used here was openly available, though broader access terms are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: Benchmark and Reference Trajectory or Network Datasets
description: A comprehensive, long-running record of terrorist attacks worldwide (over 125,000 incidents since 1970), repurposed in the single paper citing it here in a genuinely unusual way among the sources in this document: not as any measure of human movement at all, but as a location-event sequence -- treating a sequence of attacks by the same organization at different locations as directly analogous to an individual's sequence of check-ins, and applying the exact same spatio-temporal recurrent neural network architecture used elsewhere in the same paper for predicting a person's next Gowalla check-in location to instead predict which province or state a given organization is likely to attack next. This is included in this document because of that direct methodological parallel to human mobility prediction, not because it describes any actual movement of people.
accessibility_description: A publicly released, openly accessible research database.

section: Benchmark and Reference Trajectory or Network Datasets
description: A real-world peer-to-peer file-sharing network topology (a 2002 snapshot from the Stanford SNAP dataset collection, roughly 6,300 nodes and 20,800 edges), used in the single paper citing it here not as mobility data of any kind, but purely as a real-world, non-random ('scale-free') network structure to test an epidemic source-localization algorithm -- identifying where a simulated infection or piece of information most likely started, given only which nodes were observed to be affected. Its inclusion in this document reflects its role as a structural test network for algorithms of the same general type used in mobility-and-epidemic research, not any connection to human movement.
accessibility_description: A publicly released academic network dataset, via the Stanford SNAP collection.

section: Miscellaneous Sources
description: A large European electric-vehicle demonstration program, used in the single paper citing it here to derive statistical parameters of electric-vehicle driving behavior -- one of the few sources in this document specifically about how mobility patterns differ by vehicle type. Drawing on nearly 165,000 recorded driving and charging events from 457 electric vehicles across six European demonstration regions (2011-2013), the paper finds electric vehicles in this sample show a notably shorter characteristic daily travel distance (roughly 24 km) than conventional vehicles measured via floating-car GPS data in the same era (34-38 km). The paper is careful to flag that this difference may not reflect anything fundamental about electric vehicles as such: the sample itself has a real urban-driving bias, and the specific EV models observed were almost entirely small (segment A) cars, while the conventional-vehicle comparison data covered a wider range of vehicle sizes and included more extra-urban driving -- meaning some of the observed gap likely reflects who was driving what kind of car in this early EV-adoption period, not an inherent EV mobility pattern.
accessibility_description: Data from a European Commission-funded demonstration program; not a public dataset.

section: Miscellaneous Sources
description: A US research cohort focused on aging in minority populations, contributing part of the combined 139-person sample used in the single paper citing it here (alongside the ORCATECH entry elsewhere in this document) to study in-home mobility patterns in older adults. This source's specific contribution to that combined study is providing clinically-determined cognitive status (mild cognitive impairment classification, via a two-stage process combining algorithmic scoring and neuropsychologist review) for its portion of participants, which the broader study then relates to passively-sensed in-home movement patterns.
accessibility_description: A research cohort study; not a public dataset, access requires a research relationship.

section: Miscellaneous Sources
description: A Brazilian transport industry association, whose 2022 intercity bus capacity report is used in the single paper citing it here as one of three combined data sources (alongside road/waterway data and air travel statistics, both described elsewhere in this document) feeding a national mobility graph used to rank Brazilian cities by their strategic value as early-pathogen-detection sentinel sites -- using a classic maximum-flow network algorithm to identify roughly 5,570 cities as useful 'first-step' surveillance points based on how mobility flows through them. As with the related sources in this same combined dataset, the paper notes a shared limitation: private vehicle transport and mobility across international borders are both likely under-represented, since neither is well captured by any of the three official data sources combined here.
accessibility_description: Publicly released industry association transport statistics.

section: Miscellaneous Sources
description: A research infrastructure deploying passive in-home sensors (motion detectors across multiple rooms and door-contact sensors) in older adults' own homes, used in the single paper citing it here -- alongside the MARS cohort elsewhere in this document -- to study a combined sample of 139 older adults' in-home mobility, tracked passively over an average of roughly 206 sensor-days per participant. This is one of very few sources in this entire document measuring movement at genuinely sub-room scale within a person's own home, rather than movement between distinct places or regions. The paper found in-home mobility frequency was a highly reliable measure across the study population (excellent reliability), and specifically linked reduced day-to-day stability in movement patterns (though not frequency itself) to a clinical diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment -- a genuinely substantive health-relevant finding drawn directly from passive mobility sensing. Two specific limitations are worth noting: the analysis deliberately excluded data collected during the COVID-19 period (when in-home behavior would be systematically atypical), and the reported estimates describe the population on average rather than reliable estimates for any given individual.
accessibility_description: Passive in-home sensor data from a dedicated research infrastructure; not a public dataset, access requires a research relationship.

section: Miscellaneous Sources
description: An official traffic-incident data feed (used here for Greater London), used in the single paper citing it here to test whether geotagged tweets can substitute for, or usefully complement, authoritative traffic-disruption records. Comparing nearly 180,000 official traffic disruption records against roughly 63,000 geotagged tweets over one month, the paper finds the correlation between the two sources depends sharply on the *type* of disruption: tweets tracked special events fairly well (correlation 0.73), tracked ordinary traffic incidents moderately (0.59), tracked hazard-related disruptions weakly (0.41), and showed essentially no relationship at all for routine traffic-volume or construction-related disruptions (correlation as low as 0.10) -- a clear, quantified illustration that social media can be a reasonable proxy for some categories of real-world disruption and essentially useless for others, not a uniformly good or bad substitute across the board.
accessibility_description: An official transport-authority data feed; specific access terms are not detailed in the citing paper.

section: Miscellaneous Sources
description: A market-research and polling company, whose weekly US survey estimates of face-mask wearing prevalence (averaging roughly 54% across the study period) are used in the single paper citing it here -- combined with Google Trends search-volume data (see elsewhere in this document) -- to estimate mask-wearing rates at the level of individual US metropolitan statistical areas for a COVID-19 intervention-effect model.
accessibility_description: A commercial survey/polling company; specific access terms for this research use are not detailed in the citing paper.

dataset_name: FRED (A Framework for Reconstructing Epidemiological Dynamics)
section: Simulation and Synthetic-Population Tools
description: Note: this is a simulation/generation tool, not a raw real-world dataset. FRED is an open-source agent-based epidemic simulation platform (developed at the University of Pittsburgh's Public Health Dynamics Laboratory), used in the single paper citing it here to generate synthetic epidemic simulation outputs across many different parameter combinations, which then serve as training data for a much faster Gaussian-process surrogate model -- FRED's own synthetic population is itself built from RTI International and US Census-derived data, layering a generative tool on top of already-real demographic inputs. The specific application here (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania) spans both an infectious-disease model and a separate opioid-use-disorder model, illustrating this tool's use beyond infectious disease specifically.
accessibility_description: An open-source simulation platform, freely available.

section: Simulation and Synthetic-Population Tools
description: Note: this is a simulation/generation tool, not a raw real-world dataset. UrbanPop generates large synthetic populations with detailed daily activity schedules, used in the single paper citing it here to build a synthetic Utah population (roughly 3.1 million individuals, 1.04 million households, over 1,500 schools and 101,000 workplaces) for large-scale agent-based population-health simulation scaling experiments. The generation method statistically matches real American Community Survey microdata to build realistic households, then merges in real travel-diary cohorts (from the National Household Travel Survey, described elsewhere in this document) to assign realistic daily activity patterns. One specific, concrete limitation is worth flagging: the tool's normal approach to classifying areas as urban or rural relies on a proprietary commercial dataset (Claritas), which this paper's Utah application could not access, and had to approximate using the National Household Travel Survey instead -- a workaround that may make this specific application's urban/rural classification somewhat less precise than UrbanPop's typical output.
accessibility_description: A synthetic-population generation tool; specific access terms are not detailed in the citing paper, and it depends in part on a proprietary commercial data source (Claritas) for one of its standard classification steps.

dataset_name: Lausanne Data Collection Campaign / Nokia Mobile Data Challenge (LDCC/MDC)
section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description:
A long-running Swiss smartphone data collection effort centered on Lausanne, combining GPS, WiFi, and automatic place-detection sensor logs. This entry merges what were previously three separate register rows -- 'Lausanne Data Collection Campaign (LDCC)', 'Nokia Mobile Data Challenge', and 'MDC dataset' -- after direct verification confirmed all three describe the same underlying data collection: LDCC is the umbrella, multi-year campaign itself (185 users tracked over 19 months, 2009-2011, via Nokia N95 phones); the Nokia Mobile Data Challenge (MDC) is an official curated subset/track released from that same campaign for a research competition. The determination is based on direct textual evidence, not just similarity of scale: four of the five citing papers here cite the identical origin publication (Kiukkonen, Blom, Dousse, Gatica-Perez & Laurila, 'Towards Rich Mobile Phone Datasets: Lausanne Data Collection Campaign,' ICPS 2010) as the source of their data, and one paper states outright that the MDC 'originates from' LDCC. The varying participant counts reported across papers (185, 170, 80, 50, 191) are explained explicitly in the source texts as different official releases/subsets of one campaign, not different datasets -- one paper even states directly that the full 170-participant LDCC release was itself subset down to 50 users specifically for the MDC challenge task.

This dataset offers an unusually detailed, quantified illustration of how much privacy protection can cost in terms of usable data precision: of the roughly 22 million raw location samples collected, 41.8% had already been k-anonymized (spatially truncated to no better than 100m precision) before reaching researchers. The processing pipeline used to make this data usable for route analysis -- map-matching raw points onto the road network via a Hidden Markov Model, then filling short gaps using shortest-path routing, then extracting discrete 'stay points' -- is itself fairly elaborate, reflecting how much post-processing this kind of long-duration but partially degraded GPS trace requires before it becomes analytically usable. No independent ground truth was available to directly validate how accurate the resulting map-matched routes and stay points actually are.

Applications across the MDC-side papers include next-place prediction (a Markov-chain approach roughly matching, though modestly outperforming, a simple most-common-place baseline), state-space reduction methods for compressing location representations while preserving mobility-pattern fidelity, unsupervised discovery of significant locations purely from WiFi access-point co-occurrence patterns (deliberately without any labeled ground truth or access-point coordinates), and Monte Carlo simulation-based multi-step location and timing prediction. Two specific, quantified methodological artifacts recur across these papers: the dataset's place-detection algorithm uses a 20-minute minimum-stay threshold, which one paper notes explicitly excludes short-duration real destinations like bus stops or metro stations from the data entirely; and a daily automatic phone reset in the data-collection software created a spurious spike of apparent 'visits' around 3-4am every night -- a collection artifact, not a real behavioral pattern.
accessibility_description: Smartphone GPS/WiFi data from a long-running Swiss research campaign; not a public dataset. Roughly 41.8% of raw samples were further degraded to 100m precision through k-anonymization before release, and the Mobile Data Challenge subset specifically requires participation in or agreement with the original competition, not a standing public download.

section: GPS Device and App-Based Trajectory Traces
description:
A cell-tower and Bluetooth-proximity tracking study of MIT students, faculty, and staff (split across the Sloan business school and the Media Lab), conducted via Nokia 6600 phones distributed to participants during the 2004-2005 academic year -- one of the earlier smartphone-based mobility datasets in this document, formally known as the 'Reality Mining' project (Eagle & Pentland, MIT Media Lab). This entry merges what were previously two separate register rows -- 'MIT dataset' and 'MIT Reality Dataset' -- after direct verification confirmed all four citing papers trace to the same underlying collection: two papers cite the identical companion publication verbatim (Eagle, Pentland & Lazer, 'Inferring friendship/social network structure by using mobile phone data,' PNAS 2009), a third cites a different Eagle & Pentland companion paper ('Eigenbehaviors,' 2009) describing the same dataset, and the fourth explicitly thanks Nathan Eagle and Sandy Pentland by name for 'the original MIT Reality experiments.' Reported participant counts vary across papers (94, 97, ~100, 89) because different papers apply different inclusion filters (e.g. requiring a minimum amount of usable data) to the same underlying subject pool, not because they studied different populations -- one paper explicitly frames its 89-subject figure as 'subjects who have data' drawn from the full cohort.

Used across the merged set of papers for genuinely different purposes: discovering latent daily 'routines' by combining coarse location labels with Bluetooth-detected social proximity, identifying individuals purely from the statistical signature of their cell-tower movement sequences (treating each person's location history like a distinct language, achieving identification accuracy up to roughly 85% with enough data), predicting future locations from detected 'regular trajectories,' and mining 'geographic communities' via matrix factorization of cell-tower visitation similarity.

Multiple papers flag data-quality issues specific to this dataset's particular collection era and infrastructure. One notes that location labels (Home/Work/Out/No-reception) were derived from genuinely noisy, fluctuating cell-tower readings, and that Bluetooth-detected proximity is 'a reasonable, although clearly imperfect, proxy for social interaction,' since many detected nearby devices are not real face-to-face encounters at all. Another documents a specific dataset artifact worth keeping in mind for any long-duration mobile-network study: partway through the study period, the mobile operator renamed its location-area identifiers, causing the same physical cell towers to appear as entirely new locations and sharply degrading that paper's own long-run prediction accuracy at that point. A third paper's identification method also assumes each phone was used by exactly one person throughout the study, an assumption the paper itself flags as implicit and unverified.
accessibility_description: A well-known, openly released MIT research dataset from the mid-2000s.

section: Simulation and Synthetic-Population Tools
description:
Note: this is a simulation/generation tool, not a raw real-world dataset. TRANSIMS/EpiSims is a transportation-and-contact-network simulation framework that produced a large synthetic contact network for Portland, Oregon; NDSSL (Network Dynamics and Simulation Science Laboratory, Biocomplexity Institute of Virginia Tech) is the research group that produced it. This entry merges what were previously two separate register rows -- 'NDSSL' and 'TRANSIMS/EpiSims' -- after direct verification: the NDSSL-citing paper states outright that its Portland network 'was developed as part of the transportation analysis and simulation system (TRANSIMS) project by the Network Dynamics and Simulation Science Laboratory (NDSSL) group,' directly confirming NDSSL is the lab that produced this specific TRANSIMS-based population, not an independently-generated network that merely resembles it in scale.

Flagged explicitly, on its own: the two papers report a real ~38% discrepancy in total daily contact count -- roughly 20.0 million (NDSSL paper, N=1.7x10^6 individuals) versus 27,613,194 (TRANSIMS/EpiSims paper, N=1,615,860 individuals) -- that is not fully explained by rounding alone, and likely reflects a different processing cut or contact-duration/degree threshold applied to the same underlying network (the TRANSIMS/EpiSims paper explicitly caps contacts per building at 40 per person, a modeling choice that could plausibly produce a different total than an unfiltered or differently-filtered extraction of the same raw network) rather than two genuinely different network generations.

Used in the merged papers to (a) train and validate a graph neural network approach for generating and rescaling synthetic contact networks, treating the network as a realistic reference against which generated networks are compared, and (b) build age-structured transmission-probability matrices for a smallpox behavioral-response and disease-transmission study, where the resulting contact-count distribution followed a pattern closer to a power law than a simple exponential decay. Both papers are explicit that the underlying population and its mixing patterns are artificially generated via an earlier agent-based simulation, not directly observed -- so any downstream finding reflects the simulation's own assumptions as much as real Portland behavior.
accessibility_description: A large synthetic network dataset produced by an academic research group (NDSSL); access terms for the specific Portland network are not detailed in either citing paper, though the broader TRANSIMS framework has historically had some public releases -- treat this specific dataset as restricted/not-directly-downloadable pending clearer access information.
